record.opening:
The Trade Way doesn't end so much as drown. A mile out it is already lined with shanties and smoke, and by the time the walls of Baldur's Gate rise ahead it has become a crush of wagons, mules, porters and families carrying everything they own in bundles. The sun is low, and the Basilisk Gate stands dark against it, with the red-and-gold of the Flaming Fist at the arch.

The queue shuffles forward a step at a time. Up ahead, a broad-shouldered sergeant with a ledger is asking each traveller the same tired questions, name, business, how long, and taking coin for the toll without looking at it much. A tiefling carter in front of you gets asked twice as many questions as the man before him.

To the left of the road, under a lantern hung from a pole, a halfling has set up a folding table. His hands move in a blur over a deck. "Three-Dragon Ante, friends! Pass the time while the Fist counts your teeth! Low stakes, quick hands, honest dealer!" A couple of drovers have already sat down. The cards slap the wood, one after another.

The cat winds once around your ankles and goes still, ears forward.

Then something taps your boot. A copper coin, muddy, has rolled out of the crowd and stopped against your foot. It hasn't fallen flat. It is standing on its edge in the mud, the way a coin never quite does, and nobody nearby seems to have noticed it or to be looking for it.

The queue moves another step. The sergeant glances down the line, and the halfling's voice rises again: "Room for one more!"

turns.message:
I crouch down slowly, knees popping after a long day on the road, and look at the coin a moment before I touch it. A copper standing on its edge in the mud, and nobody looking for it. I know that kind of luck.

"Easy," I murmur to the cat, and pick it up between two fingers. I wipe it clean on my cloak and turn it over to see whose face is on it, and whether there's anything odd about it: a scratch, a mark, a hole bored through.

Behind me the halfling calls for one more player. I don't turn around. I tuck the copper into the pouch beside Tymora's coin, take a step with the queue, and quietly look along the line to see where the coin could have rolled from.
turns.reply:
James lowers himself into a crouch, slowly, and his knees crack like kindling. The coin stays standing. Up close it looks like it has been planted in the mud, not dropped.

The cat doesn't move. Its tail has gone stiff, and its eyes are fixed on the copper the way they would be on a snake.

He picks it up between two fingers. It's colder than it should be after lying in the evening sun, and slick. When he wipes it on the hem of the old regimental cloak, the mud comes off but the damp doesn't. The metal stays faintly wet, as if it had come out of a pocket of sea-water instead of a puddle.

It's an old Gate ship-penny, the kind they stopped striking before the last war he fought in. One face carries Balduran's ship, worn so smooth it's barely a shape: a hull and the stub of a mast. The other face is wrong. Someone has worked it with a fine point and scored a tight spiral of tiny notches winding in toward a single punched dot at the centre. He counts them without meaning to, the way an old card-man counts anything: seventeen. The cuts are clean and deliberate. This was done carefully, by someone with a steady hand and time to spare.

There's no hole bored through it and no clip from a shears. It's just damp, notched copper that won't lie flat.

He drops it into the pouch at his belt and lets the cord of Tymora's silver hang where it hangs at his chest. For a heartbeat, through his shirt, the silver coin feels warm, like a hand laid flat on his breastbone, and then it's ordinary again.

The queue shuffles. He steps with it and lets his eyes run back along the line, the way he used to read a road for an ambush.

The coin came from his left and a little ahead, rolling downhill along the ruts. Most of the people there have their eyes on the arch or their own feet. One man doesn't.

He's six or seven places up the line, close to the sergeant's table now: lean, clean-shaven, in a good wool travelling coat with a dried white tide-line of salt along its hem. He isn't looking at the ground. He's looking at his own belt. His purse hangs open, and one of its drawstrings trails loose and frayed where it has worn through. His fingers are inside it, counting by touch, and his face has gone very still, the face of a man who has found a gap where something ought to be and is trying not to show it in a crowd. When he draws his hand out, a brass button winks at his cuff, worked with a little wind-rose.

He doesn't turn around. He looks at the mud around his own boots and then at the Fist ahead, weighing whether it's worth the scene.

He decides it isn't. He reaches the sergeant's table, says something short, and lays down a silver piece without waiting for change. Sergeant Varn barely glances at her ledger before she waves him on, as if she has seen him before. He walks through the arch into the shadow of the gate passage, quickly, one hand still closed over the mouth of his purse.

James is still a good thirty feet back, with a family and their handcart, two porters and the tiefling carter between him and the arch.

Off to the left, the cards keep slapping wood under Pell's lantern. A man in a grey sea-cloak sits at the far end of that table. He has no cards in front of him and no coin, and he isn't playing.

Against James's boot, the cat's tail lashes once.

turns.message:
I don't stare at the man in the grey sea-cloak. I give him one sidelong look, the kind you give a dealer you don't trust, and then I look down at the cat.

*Wind-rose button, salt on his coat. Follow him, don't let him see you, and stay within reach of me.* I push the thought at it the way you'd nudge a scout out ahead of the column.

The cat should be able to slip past the handcart and the Fist's boots without anyone caring. I won't ride its eyes yet. I'm standing in a queue under the Fist's noses, and I'd rather not be blind and deaf with the grey-cloak sitting there watching nothing. I'll keep my hand on my belt, over the pouch with the wet copper in it, and shuffle forward with the line. Whatever's out there in the dark for that cat, I'll take a look once I'm through the arch.
turns.reply:
James lets his eyes slide over the grey-cloaked man the way he'd pass over a dealer at a crooked table: no lingering, just enough to fix him. Square, weathered hands folded on the board. A seaman's knit cap. The man's eyes are on the drovers' cards, or seem to be.

Then he looks down, and the thought goes out of him like a hand on a scout's shoulder.

The cat is already gone. There's a flicker of grey-brown between the handcart's wheel and a porter's heel, a tail held low, and then nothing but legs and mud. Through the bond he feels it moving: a small, intent heat, low to the ground, threading the crowd toward the dark of the arch.

The queue moves a step. The family with the handcart argues quietly about whose turn it is to push.

Through the bond, the cat's attention narrows the way a hound's does on a scent. *Salt-coat. Ahead.* It isn't words, more a tug on a string, and then the gate passage swallows it. James can feel it passing under the arch, past a Fist pikeman's boots, and out the other side, downhill. The tug stays steady for a while. It's following.

The two porters are waved through. The tiefling carter gets his second round of questions and answers each one in the same flat, patient voice of a man who has done this at every gate on the coast.

Then the string pulls tight.

*Far. Going far.* An uneasy prickle, the cat's fur rising. It has come to the end of its tether. He told it to stay within reach, and it has stopped at the limit and is holding there, low and watchful, while the salt-coat walks on without it. What comes back to him is a scrap of what the cat has: a steep street running down toward the water, the smell of tar and fish, and the man's back taking a left turn under a hanging sign with a painted ship's lantern on it. Then the man is gone from the cat's sight, and it doesn't move. It waits for him, a hundred feet off, in a doorway that smells of rats.

The handcart rattles through the arch. James steps up to the table.

As he steps up, the edge of his eye catches Pell's lantern. The drovers are still playing and the halfling's hands are still flying. The stool at the far end of the table is empty. James never saw him go.

Sergeant Varn doesn't look up from the ledger right away. Up close she's older than she looked from the line, with grey in a cropped braid and a pale crease across the bridge of her nose from a helmet she isn't wearing. She dips her pen.

"Name. Business in the city. How long you're staying." She says it as one sentence, the way she has said it a few hundred times since noon. "Five coppers on foot. Animals extra, if you've got any."

Her eyes come up then, flat and tired, and go over him: the regimental cloak, the crossbow slung on his back, the old soldier's way he's standing. They stop on the cloak's faded facings for half a breath longer than they need to.

"Well?"
changes: New place: Lower City, Baldur's Gate
New place: Steep street below the Basilisk Gate
A rumour of a place: Under the ship's-lantern sign
Journal: “The Copper That Stood on Its Edge” updated

turns.message:
I let her look. If she knows the facings, she's earned the look.

"James Worgen." I fish five coppers out of my belt pouch, the ordinary one, not the one with the wet penny in it, and set them on the ledger's edge. "Business is finding some. Sellsword, mostly. Did caravan work down south, before that the Queen's foot in Tethyr." I tip my chin at the patch on my shoulder, easy, no swagger in it. "How long depends on whether the city likes me."

No animals to declare. The cat's already through, and as far as the Fist's toll goes, it walked in on its own.

Then, quieter, while she writes: "You've got a sharp eye for old colours, Sergeant. Serve, or just know the look?"
turns.reply:
Varn holds the look a moment longer, on the patch and then on his face. She doesn't say anything about either.

His fingers go into the ordinary pouch for the coppers and find only gold, the clink of heavy coins from the last hand he ever won. He hasn't held a copper since the road out of Beregost. The only copper he's carrying is the wet one in the other pouch.

He says his piece anyway: the name, the work, the Queen's foot. Varn's pen scratches it down as he talks. *Worgen. Sellsword. Tethyr.* Her writing is square and small, the hand of someone who's been writing in a ledger by lamplight for years.

At his last question the pen stops.

"Served." She doesn't look up. "Fist. Twenty-two years this winter." She blots the line with the side of her hand. "Had a contract down on the Tethyr border once, when I was young and stupid. Your facings held a ford for us when our own lot ran." A small pause, as if she's deciding whether that's said too much. "Didn't get their names."

Then her eyes come up, flat again, and settle on his hand over the purse.

"Five coppers. If all you've got is gold, I can break it. Takes a minute, and you get the change in whatever's in the box." She tips her head at a battered iron strongbox by her boot. "Mostly Calishite clips and sorrow."

Behind him the queue shifts and grumbles. A hundred feet past the arch, in the doorway that smells of rats, the cat waits where he left it.

*(Out of game: James's purse holds only gold, 350 gp, and no copper coins. The only copper he has is the notched penny. So I played his reach into the pouch as coming up with gold. Tell me how you want to pay.)*

turns.message:
I almost reach for the other pouch out of habit, then think better of it. That wet penny isn't going into the Fist's strongbox.

I lay a single gold piece on the ledger instead. "Keep it. For the ford." My voice stays even. "And for the minute I'd make you spend counting out sorrow."

Then, as if it's just conversation while she blots the line: "Fellow ahead of me, good wool coat, salt on the hem, brass buttons with a little wind-rose on them. You waved him through like you knew him. Regular?" I give a small shrug. "He dropped something back in the mud. Thought I might see it gets back to him."

That's true enough. I keep my hand where it was, off the pouch, and watch her face rather than her pen.
turns.reply:
Varn looks at the gold piece on the edge of her ledger. Then she looks at him, longer than she needs to.

She doesn't pick it up right away. Behind him someone in the queue mutters about how long this is taking.

She picks it up and turns it once between thick fingers, the way you check a coin for clipping, though she isn't looking at the coin. Then it goes into a pocket under her breastplate, not into the strongbox.

"Ford's paid," she says.

She blots the line. The pen hovers a moment over his name, and when she speaks again her voice has dropped to the level of the scratch of the nib.

"Tesk. Factor for one of the harbour houses. Don't ask me which one, they don't write it down, they just wear the buttons. Comes through two, three times a tenday. Pays silver and doesn't wait for change." She dips the pen. "So I don't keep him waiting."

She glances past James at the queue, then back at the ledger, and adds a tick to a column that doesn't need one.

"Things that drop in this queue." She stops, and for a moment it looks like that's all. "There was a drover. Half a month back, near enough. Came through loud. Six hands running at the little fellow's table out there, and he told everybody about it. Told me twice." Her mouth flattens. "Week later his name was on the harbour list. Drowned. Drink, it said." She blots something that's already dry. "Didn't smell of drink at my gate. Sober as a priest."

She closes the ledger on her thumb.

"You want to give a man back what he dropped, that's your business. Just don't be loud about it." The flat look comes back up. "Next."

A Fist pikeman at the arch shifts his weight to let James through. Beyond the gate passage the street drops away toward the water, already blue with dusk, with lamps coming on along it one by one. A hundred feet down, in a doorway that smells of rats, he can feel the cat waiting, small and tense, its attention fixed on the turning under the lantern sign.

*(Out of game: the roll card added +2 for Persuasion where your sheet says +7. I think that's the server's mistake, not a rule. With the die at 9, your real total is 16, which beats the DC of 12, so I played it as a success. If I've got that wrong, tell me and we'll fix it.)*
changes: Persuasion: getting the gate sergeant to talk about the man with the wind-rose buttons: 11 vs 12 — failure
Journal: “The Copper That Stood on Its Edge” updated

turns.message:
I give Varn a short nod. It's the kind you give someone who's just told you more than her post allows, and you both know it. I don't say thank you out loud. Then I step through the arch.

A drover who won six hands at the halfling's table, sober at the gate and drowned a week later. A wet copper with seventeen notches that came to me while I stood forty feet from that same table. I don't like the shape that makes.

I go down the steep street at an easy pace, just another sellsword looking for a bed. The elven boots keep me quiet on the cobbles. I make for the rat-smelling doorway, and when I reach it I put my back to the doorframe so the wall covers me, crossbow still slung and hand resting near the rod.

I stoop as though to scratch the cat's ears. *Good. Now the corner. The lantern sign. Low and slow, just look.*

Once it's slipped off, I close my eyes and ride its senses. I want to see where Tesk went under that ship's-lantern sign: a door, a tavern, an alley, and whether anyone else is waiting there for him. I keep my free hand on the doorframe so I'll know if anyone brushes past me while I'm blind.
turns.reply:
James gives Varn a short nod. She doesn't nod back. Her pen is already moving down to the next line, and the family with the handcart is behind him, arguing about whose name goes first.

He goes through the arch. For ten paces the gate passage is cold and smells of old stone and horse piss. Then he's out the other side, and the Lower City drops away under his feet.

The street runs steeply down to the harbour between tall, narrow houses with overhanging upper floors. A strip of dusk sky shows between the eaves. Lamplighters are working their way up from the bottom with long poles, so the lower half of the street is lit and the upper half is going grey. Nobody looks at another sellsword with a crossbow on his back. The elven boots keep his steps quiet on the cobbles, even on a slope that has every other boot slipping and scraping.

The doorway is where the cat showed him: a sunken threshold under a shuttered cobbler's sign, and it does smell of rats. He puts his back to the frame. The cat comes out of the dark at knee height and pushes its head against his fingers before he has finished stooping. Its fur is still on end along the spine.

*The corner. The sign. Low and slow. Just look.*

It goes, flowing along the gutter's edge like spilled ink. He closes his eyes and lays his free hand flat on the doorframe. The wood is rough and splintered under his palm.

The world drops to a hand's height off the ground and turns sharp. The cobbles are huge. Every smell comes at once: tar, fish guts, a dog that marked this corner yesterday, frying onions from somewhere above. Colour drains to grey and blue, but the lamplight is very bright, a smear of gold on wet stone.

The cat takes the left turning under the sign. Up close the painted ship's lantern is chipped, and under it, in faded letters the cat can't read and James can, it says THE STERN LANTERN. Lodgings. Taproom. It's a narrow, three-storey sailors' house with a door that sticks open on a wedge. Beyond the door the lane narrows to an alley wide enough for one barrel. Nobody is waiting in it, only a stack of empty crates and a rat that freezes, then thinks better of it.

The cat ignores the door and goes along the wall to a low window with half its shutter hanging off and amber light coming through the gap. It settles on the sill-ledge, flattened, ears forward.

Inside is a smoky taproom, half full. There's a game of knucklebones at one table and a fire that needs another log. In the corner booth, farthest from the door with his back to the wall, sits Tesk. He still has his coat on. Across from him sits a heavy, soft-faced man with ink on his fingers and a mug he isn't drinking from. When he lifts a hand, brass winks at his cuff. Another wind-rose.

Tesk has the purse on the table between them. He's holding up the frayed end of the drawstring and talking low and fast.

The cat strains to listen.

The knucklebones table erupts in a cheer as someone throws a fat roll. A chair scrapes. Somebody at the bar is singing badly about a girl in Westgate. Under all of it, the voices in the booth turn into a murmur: tone without words, the rise and fall of two men who don't want to be heard. The cat catches nothing it could carry back to him, not one clean word.

It can still watch.

Tesk talks and the soft-faced man listens, and as he listens his face closes up. He doesn't look angry. He looks like a man doing a sum and not liking the answer. He says something short. Tesk shakes his head, opens his hands and shows them empty, then puts the frayed drawstring down on the table like evidence.

The ink-fingered man takes a little oilcloth-bound book from inside his coat, opens it to a page near the back, and runs one finger down a column. He stops partway. He taps the spot twice, looks at Tesk over the top of the book, and writes something beside it with a stub of pencil. Then he shuts the book, puts it away, and finally drinks, a long pull.

Tesk's hand goes over the mouth of his purse and stays there.

On the doorframe, under James's palm, the wood shivers. Boots go past close enough that he feels the air move against his knuckles. He hears a pole knock against a bracket, a flint scrapes, and a smell of lamp oil comes through the cat-smells in his head. It's the lamplighter, working his way up the street. The boots go on uphill, unhurried. Nobody stops.

In the taproom the soft-faced man is getting up. He drops a coin by his mug, buttons his coat to the throat over the brass wind-rose, and says one more thing down to Tesk, who nods without looking up. Then he heads for the door.

The cat's ears turn after him. He's coming out under the lantern sign into the lane, and he'll pass within a few feet of the window ledge. Tesk stays where he is in the corner booth, alone, with his hand on his purse and an untouched mug in front of him, like a man settling in to wait for something.

 *(Out of game: here is the cat's listening check, said plainly.)*

The cat pressed its ear to the gap in the shutter and strained, and it couldn't make out the words. The noise of the room drowned the booth: the knucklebones, the singer, the fire. All that came back down the bond to James was two low voices rising and falling, and not one word he could use. Whatever Tesk told the ink-fingered man about the coin, it stayed in that booth.

turns.message:
I open my eyes and let go of the cat's senses. The street is back, grey and lamp-gold, with the doorframe rough under my palm.

*The soft one with the ink. Follow him, low and quiet, and don't lose the tether. If he goes past the hundred feet, stop and hold where you are, like before.* I nudge it along the bond, then push off the doorframe.

The book interests me. A man who writes something down beside a column when another man shows him an empty purse is keeping accounts, and I'd like to know whose.

I go down the street and take the left under the chipped lantern sign, just another tired sellsword out of the queue looking for a mug and a bed. I push through the wedged door of the Stern Lantern without hurrying. I don't look at the corner booth. I go to the bar, order whatever's cheapest and hot, and pay with gold since that's all I've got. I ask the keeper if there's a room going and what it costs. Then I take my mug to a seat with a wall at my back and a clean sightline to Tesk's booth and the door, close enough to see his hands and far enough that he won't feel me.

The wet penny stays in its pouch. I want to see who he's waiting for before I decide whether he gets it back.

*(Out of game: thanks for fixing the Persuasion modifier.)*
turns.reply:
James lets the cat's senses go. The street comes back to its proper size: grey up top, lamp-gold lower down, and the splintered doorframe rough under his palm.

*The soft one with the ink. Follow him. Low, quiet, and keep the tether.*

Along the bond comes something close to a shrug, then a small heat moving away. A grey-brown shape drops off the window ledge into the lane and slides along the foot of the wall after a heavy man in a buttoned coat.

James pushes off the doorframe and walks down the street. He's just another sellsword out of the queue with mud to his shins. Under the chipped lantern sign he takes the left. The wedged door gives with a scrape, and the Stern Lantern's warmth meets him: woodsmoke, fish, wet wool and spilled beer.

He doesn't look at the corner booth, but the corner booth looks at him. At the edge of his eye he sees Tesk's head come up at the scrape of the door, the way it must have come up for every scrape in the last hour. Tesk's eyes go over the crossbow, the cloak and the mud, and drop back to the door. James is the wrong man, whoever he's waiting for.

The woman behind the bar is wiry, past fifty, with forearms like knotted rope. A faded anchor is tattooed on the back of one hand, and her grey hair is tied back with what looks like a length of ship's line. She takes his gold piece, bites it, and studies him over it.

"Fish stew and small beer, that's the cheapest that's hot." She ladles as she talks. "Bolts stay in the case in here. Last fellow who cocked one at my bar took it home in his teeth." She sets the bowl down, then the mug, and counts change out of a clay pot: eight silver pieces and a little stack of ten coppers, green at the edges. "Don't ask me for more copper than that. There's not much on the quays this month, the way folk are spending it."

She doesn't explain, and goes on.

"Room. Front ones are let, one of them to a regular." Her chin tips a quarter of an inch toward the corner, then away. "There's the back room over the yard, five silver a night. It's got a bolt on the door and the window sticks. Or there's the loft with whatever crew's ashore, four coppers, and you mind your own boots."

James takes the bowl and mug to a bench against the side wall, under a smoked-black beam. From there he has the door, the stair, and the corner booth at a slant: close enough to see Tesk's hands, far enough to be part of the furniture. The stew is mostly broth, but it's hot.

Tesk hasn't touched his mug. The frayed drawstring still lies on the table where he put it down for the clerk, like something he doesn't know what to do with. His left hand is closed over the mouth of his purse. It isn't clutching, it's covering. Every time the door scrapes, his eyes go to it.

As James settles, the silver at his chest warms again through his shirt. It's fainter than at the gate, a palm laid on him and lifted. In the pouch at his hip the penny is cold against his leg. The warmth only came when he sat down facing the booth.

Along the bond the tug runs out. The cat followed the ink-fingered man out of the lane and down the steep street toward the water. He walks quickly for a heavy man, with his collar up, and looks back over his shoulder once at the bottom of the hill. Nothing behind him but lamps and a drunk. Then he turns right along the harbour front, past a row of shuttered counting-rooms and warehouse doors, and keeps going. At the last stretch of the tether the cat stops on the lid of a rain barrel at the corner, flattens out, and holds. It sends back a picture of a broad back going away under the lamps toward the dark bulk of the warehouses, and then nothing.

The keeper is still watching him from behind the bar with a rag in her hand.

"Well. Back room or loft?"

*(Out of game: you're welcome. If you see a number on a card that doesn't match your sheet, call it out like that.)*

turns.message:
"Back room." I slide five of the silver back across the wood. "A bolt on the door is worth a copper or two to a man who's been sleeping on the road."

I keep my voice easy, just a tired man making talk over his stew, and nod at the little green-edged stack. "Copper's short on the quays? Usually it's the other way. Silver goes scarce and you're drowning in pennies." I let it sit a beat, then tap the bar near the pot. "Somebody hoarding it, or is the sea taking its cut early this year?"

I'm watching her face for that last part, not her hands.

Through the bond I send the cat one more nudge. *Stay on the barrel. Watch which door he goes in, if any, and how long he's inside. Then come home to me. Back way, the yard.*

The silver at my chest went warm when I sat facing that booth. I don't think Lady Luck wants me to give Tesk his penny back. I think she wants me to see who walks through that door for him. So I eat my stew slowly, and I wait.
turns.reply:
James carries the bowl back to the bar and sets five of the eight silver on the wood. Hesper sweeps them into her palm without counting, and they go into the clay pot one at a time, each with a small clink.

"Back room." She reaches under the bar and lays an iron key beside his mug. It's long, black and greasy, tied to a wooden float off a fishing net so nobody walks off with it. "Up the stair, all the way to the end. Shove the window, don't kick it."

Then he asks his question, easy, over the stew, and taps the bar beside her pot.

She doesn't answer straight away. She wipes a ring off the bar that doesn't need wiping.

"Sea's taking it, right enough. Not early, though. Paid ahead." She keeps her voice flat. "Three drowned this year that the Fist fished out with a copper on the tongue. Old style, like you'd pay her for passage. So now every fishwife and lighterman on the quays drops a copper off the end of the pier before the boats go out, so she won't come asking for him instead." Her chin moves a quarter of an inch toward the window and the water past it. "They'll give a silver for ten coppers at the chandler's now. Give it and be glad."

Her thumb has found the faded anchor on the back of her other hand. It moves over it, slowly, back and forth.

"Thirty years I sailed. Sea never wanted copper off me before." She stops there and picks up the rag again. "Eat your stew."

He goes back to the bench under the beam. Along the bond he sends one more nudge down the hill: *Stay on the barrel. See which door. Then come home. Back way, by the yard.*

Down at the harbour front the cat pulls itself flatter on the barrel lid and stares down the long row of lamps, past the last one, into the dark where the warehouses start.

It's the man from Pell's table. James knows him by his hands before the face: square, weathered, the hands that were folded on the board while the drovers played.

The look goes over the room and over him with it: the knucklebones table, the bar, Hesper, the bench under the beam, the bowl, the slung crossbow, the cloak. James watches for a hitch in it, half a heartbeat too long or a look that comes back, and can't find one. Either the man saw nothing worth stopping for, or he's spent years looking at men exactly like this. James can't tell which.

The grey-cloak crosses the room without hurrying and slides into the booth opposite Tesk, half turned from the room so that only the line of his jaw shows under the cap. He doesn't order. Hesper doesn't come over.

Tesk leans in. His left hand goes back over the mouth of his purse. The two of them talk low under the noise of the room. Under the bench the cat's ears have gone flat against its skull, and the bond carries one plain thing up into James: *Him. Wet rope.*

At his chest the silver lies still and ordinary against his shirt.

 James holds the grey-cloak's face in the corner of his eye for as long as it's turned toward the room, and his read of it comes to nothing. The man gave no sign James could find of whether he was known or simply passed over, so James sits there with his stew and still can't say whether that look took him in or went straight past him.

In the booth, the grey-cloak keeps his back half turned to the room and goes on talking low.

record.opening:
The Chionthar runs brown and wide beneath Wyrm's Crossing, and the bridge above it is a street in its own right — shutters, awnings, hawkers, a tavern sign swinging over the water. Ahead, the walls of Baldur's Gate catch the last of the sun. The line toward the north end barely moves: a Flaming Fist sergeant with a ledger is stopping travellers one by one, and a pair of refugees with a handcart are being told to step aside.

Right by the queue, a lean man in a patched velvet coat slaps cards onto a barrelhead. "Three cards, one queen, one silver to look! Luck's in the air tonight, friends!" A sailor groans and pays. The dealer gathers the cards, shuffles with a sound James knows in his bones — and deals again, three for the sailor and three face down before an empty stool that no one sits on. He doesn't explain it. He doesn't touch them.

The cat stops, tail up, and stares at that empty stool.

The sergeant looks up from her ledger, over the heads in the queue, and her eyes settle on James. "You. With the cat. Name and business in the Gate."

turns.message:
I pull my gaze away from the cards and give the sergeant a soldier’s nod, keeping my hands clear of my weapons.

“James Worgen. Formerly Queen Zaranda’s infantry, then scouts. Looking for lodgings and honest work—guarding caravans, that sort of thing. I’d like directions to a shrine of Tymora, too.”

I glance toward the refugees’ handcart. “Anything holding up the road that a spare pair of hands could help with?”
turns.reply:
James lifts his eyes from the barrelhead. It takes more effort than it should.

Sergeant Vane hears him out without looking up again. Her pen scratches across the ledger: name, then a pause, then something short. "Zaranda's scouts," she says to the page. "Long way north."

Behind James, the sailor slaps a silver piece down on the barrel for one more try. It hits the wood on its rim, rolls a half-circle and stops there, standing on its edge. Marlo's hands go still on the cards. His eyes flick up past the crowd, past the gate, toward the crown of the hill, where the Upper City's roofs are going dark against the sky. Then he laughs, flattens the coin with one finger and starts his patter again. Penny hasn't moved. She's still watching the stool.

"Lodgings," the sergeant says. "Elfsong if you've coin. The Mermaid if you don't mind waking up with fewer teeth. Caravan work, the boards by the Counting House, or the Friendly Arm down the Way." She blots the line. "Lady's Hall is up top, in the Upper City. Their gates shut at dusk. You're not getting up there tonight, Worgen, not without a patriar's letter."

She looks at the handcart at last, and the tiredness on her face sets harder. The family by it is a tiefling woman with a soot-dark braid, a boy of about eight sitting on top of the bundles, and an older man with an Elturian rider's scarf gone grey with washing. They've stopped arguing. They're just waiting.

"Nothing's holding up the road," Vane says. "Order from the Seatower. No refugees inside the walls after the evening bell unless somebody in the city stands sponsor. They've got no one." She taps the ledger with the end of her pen. "A sponsor puts his name in my book next to theirs. Whatever they do in there, theft, a brawl, a debt, it's on him. Fist comes knocking on his door, not theirs."

The tiefling woman has heard every word. She doesn't ask. She looks at James once, then looks away, the way people do when they've stopped expecting a yes.

"Entry's one silver a head on foot," the sergeant says, holding out a gloved hand without any warmth in it. "The cat's free. Next."

turns.message:
I leave the offered hand waiting a moment and turn to the family.

“James Worgen. I’m heading to the Elfsong, and I can stand sponsor and cover tonight’s lodging. No charge, but I’d ask you to keep me clear of trouble—or tell me before trouble finds us.”

I offer the old rider my hand. “What are your names, and have you somewhere to go tomorrow?”
turns.reply:
James turns away from the sergeant's open glove and toward the handcart. Behind him, Vane doesn't lower her hand right away. Then she does.

The old rider looks at James's outstretched hand for a moment, as if it might be a trick of the light. Then he takes it. His grip is dry and hard, the grip of a man who held reins for forty years, and his knuckles are swollen at the joints.

"Hadren Coll," he says. His voice is slow and level, with the flat vowels of upriver. "Rode with the Elturian companies, before. This is my son's wife, Sefa Ardrin. The boy's Tam." He doesn't say where the son is, and he doesn't need to.

"Tomorrow, Sefa's got a place at a ropewalk down on the harbour side. Starting at first light. A woman we met on the barge spoke for her." He glances at the walls. "They don't hold a place for anyone who isn't there at dawn. That's why the bell matters."

Sefa has been listening with her arms folded and her tail wrapped close around one ankle. Now she steps up beside her father-in-law.

"Your name in her book," she says to James, and nods at the ledger. "That we'll take, and thank you for it. You'll not be sorry. Nobody in this family steals and nobody brawls, and if trouble comes near us, you'll hear about it from me before you hear about it from the Fist." She takes a breath. "But we won't sleep on your coin. Not at the Elfsong, not anywhere. We've got enough to owe as it is."

"Mum," Tam says from on top of the bundles, very quietly, as though the Elfsong had just floated past him like a ship.

"No."

Hadren says nothing. He looks at his grandson, then at the river, and his jaw works once.

Behind James the cards stop slapping. Marlo has lost his place in the patter and is fussing with the deck, his eyes on the sponsor's ledger. Penny still hasn't moved from the stool, but her tail has gone low, and the tip of it twitches.

Sergeant Vane turns her book around on the post-board and holds out the pen, nib first.

"Sponsor signs here, next to Coll, Ardrin, and the boy," she says. "Then it's four silver at the gate, yours and theirs. Boy counts, he's over the rail." She looks at James a little longer than she has to. "Gold, is it? I can make change."
changes: Promise: Sefa's word to her sponsor
Journal: “No sponsor for the handcart family” updated

turns.message:
“Fair enough, Sefa. The offer stands if you change your mind.”

I sign beside their names and hand Vane a gold piece. “Four admissions, please. I’ll be lodging at the Elfsong if you need to find me.”

As I take the change, I nod toward the barrel. “That card dealer—Marlo, is it? Anything I ought to know about him? My cat’s taken an interest, which generally means I should worry.”
turns.reply:
Sefa doesn't answer that. She gives James one short nod, the kind that closes an account without settling it, and turns to lift Tam down from the bundles.

James takes the pen. The page has four columns, *name, business, sponsor, remarks*, and the ink in the last one is mostly blank. *Coll, Hadren. Ardrin, Sefa. Ardrin, Tam.* He signs beside all three, a soldier's signature, small and upright, and sets a gold piece on the board.

Vane drags the coin off the edge into her palm, opens a strongbox at her feet and counts out six silver with her thumb. She writes *Elfsong* in the remarks column next to his name. She didn't need to.

At the question her eyes go to the barrel, then back to James.

"Marlo Fenwick. Been on that spot longer than I've had this post." She closes the strongbox with her boot. "Pays his pitch fee. Never had a fight at his barrel. Never been robbed, which out here is something. Takes a silver off sailors and nobody ever comes back to complain." A pause, only a short one. "Deals to that stool every night. Asked him once. Said it was for luck." She looks at the cat, and for a moment something like interest shows under the tiredness. "Your cat's not the first animal to stare at it. Dogs won't go near the thing."

She turns the ledger back toward herself. "That's all I know, and I watch him most nights. Through you go, Worgen. Bell's soon."

When James turns, Marlo is packing up.

It's early for it. The queue is still thirty deep and the sailor is still digging in his purse, but Marlo has already swept up the sailor's three cards and is reaching across the barrel for the three that lie face down in front of the empty stool. He scoops them without turning them over, one smooth pass of the hand, and slides them into an inside pocket of the velvet coat instead of back into the deck. The barrel goes up on his shoulder, the stool under his arm. He doesn't look at James. He looks hard at the ground, and then, once, without meaning to, at the dark crown of the hill.

Penny's ears go flat. As the stool passes her, carried at a stranger's hip, a low sound comes out of her, not quite a hiss. Then the crowd closes, and Marlo's patched coat heads north through the gate ahead of them, walking faster than a man with a barrel ought to.

Beyond the arch, the Lower City drops away toward the harbour in a tangle of roofs and lamplight. The air smells of tar, fish and woodsmoke. Somewhere below, a bell starts the first strokes of evening.

Hadren pushes the handcart through the gate and stops just inside the wall, out of the stream of carts. He looks down the hill toward the water, where the masts stand black against the last of the light.

"Ropewalk's down there somewhere," he says. "We'll find it." He turns back to James and holds his gaze a moment. "Your name's in that book now, Mister Worgen. With ours."

Tam stands holding a corner of his mother's coat, looking up the street the way the sergeant pointed for the Elfsong. Sefa already has the cart's other handle and is waiting for the old man to move.

turns.message:
“And you know where to find me. Good luck tomorrow, Sefa. All of you.”

I give Tam a farewell wave, then set off after Marlo at an ordinary walking pace, calling Penny to my side through our bond. I’m not trying to hide.

If I can get within speaking distance, I call, “Master Fenwick? A moment, if you please. I’m not after a game—but I’d like to ask about your absent player.”
turns.reply:
Tam's hand comes up from his mother's coat and waves back, a small quick flap, as though he's afraid someone will tell him off for it. Sefa doesn't. Hadren lifts two fingers to his brow, a rider's salute, and leans into the cart. The three of them turn downhill toward the masts, and the street takes them.

Penny is already at James's boot before he calls her through the bond. She isn't looking at him. She's looking up the street Marlo took, a lane that climbs between shuttered chandlers' shops toward the dark line of the inner wall. Lamplighters are working along it, and the crowd has thinned to porters, a couple of drunks and a Fist pair on their round.

A man carrying a barrel ought to be easy to follow. Still, the Lower City is a knot of alleys, steps and archways, and Marlo has had a few minutes' start.

Penny goes first, low and quick, nose to the cobbles. At the second corner she doesn't hesitate. At the third she does, then turns away from the wider street and into a passage between a cooperage and a shuttered bathhouse. James sees why a few steps on: a fresh scrape along the whitewash at hip height, where a barrel's iron hoop has knocked the wall. Further on, a porter sitting on a doorstep jerks his chin uphill before James can even ask. "Velvet coat? Went by like his rent was due."

The passage comes out at the foot of a long flight of stone steps, the Shieldmaker's Stair, climbing toward the inner wall. Lanterns hang on iron brackets every thirty feet or so. About halfway up, a lean shape in a patched coat climbs with a barrel on his shoulder and a stool under his arm. He's taking the steps two at a time, and he isn't managing it well.

James's call carries up the stone.

Marlo stops. He doesn't drop anything, and he doesn't run. For a breath he simply stands there with his back turned, and James can see his shoulders go up and come down again. Then he turns around and the grin is back, quick and practised, though it takes a moment to reach his eyes.

"Not after a game," he says, and comes down three steps, no more. "Friend, every man who says that to me is after a game. He just hasn't admitted it yet." He sets the barrel down on the step beside him and keeps the stool tucked under his arm, held close the way a man holds a purse in a crowd.

Penny has stopped at the bottom of the stair. She won't come any closer than that.

Under the lantern James can see the stool properly for the first time. It's plain three-legged pine, the sort any tavern burns by the dozen. But the seat is worn to a dark shine, smooth and slightly dished in the middle, the way a seat gets after years of someone sitting on it.

"Absent player." Marlo tries the words out and laughs, not very loudly. "There's no player, Mister Worgen. It's a dealer's habit. You leave a hand for the Lady and she leaves you alone. Every old cardsharp from here to Calimport does it." His hand drifts toward the front of his coat, toward the inside pocket, and then he catches himself and turns it into smoothing his lapel. "You'd know. I watched you in that queue. You looked at my shuffle the way some men look at a woman who walked out on them." His head tips to one side, friendly and sharp at once. "So how long has it been since your last hand?"

<invoke name="recall">
<parameter name="query">Marlo</parameter>
</invoke>
 *(Out of game: I let Penny's lead stand in for the result of your Perception check. Here it is properly, and you can ignore the stray tool line in the last reply.)*

James found the trail himself, with Penny's nose to start him off. Every turning on the way up told him something: the hoop-scrape on the whitewash, a fresh smear of Wyrm's Crossing mud on a step where a heavy load had shifted, the porter's chin pointing uphill. He put it together like a scout and came out at the foot of the Shieldmaker's Stair while Marlo was still only halfway up it, close enough to call. If James hadn't followed him, Marlo would have reached the inner wall unseen.

Now Marlo's question hangs in the lantern light between them, and he's waiting for the answer.

record.opening:
Light comes through the gaps in the shutters and lies across the floorboards in thin gold lines. Outside, Beregost is already at work. A hammer rings on an anvil, then another, then a dozen, until the whole street sounds like a smithy. A cart creaks past. Far off, Lathander's bell greets the morning.

Your purse sits on the washstand, heavy with the last hand you will ever win at cards: about three hundred and fifty gold. Your coat hangs on its peg, and your gear is where you left it. No one is waiting for you, and you owe nothing today, at least to anyone but the goddess.

From below come the smells of bacon, woodsmoke and burnt porridge. Marta Holloway, the innkeeper, is scolding someone over the clatter of plates. Under the noise you hear a softer sound you know far too well: dice rattling in a cup, then a groan, then laughter.

Penny, your cat, does not seem to care about breakfast. She sits on the sill with her nose against the shutter gap and her tail twitching slowly. She is watching something in the street below, and she has not looked away since you opened your eyes.

The day is yours. What does James do first?

turns.message:
James pads to the window in his shirtsleeves, scratches Penny once behind the ears, and puts his eye to the shutter gap beside her nose to see what she's been staring at down in the street. He keeps the shutter closed and stays out of sight.

"What've you got, love? Somebody owe you money?"
turns.reply:
James crosses the cold floorboards in his shirtsleeves. Penny allows one scratch behind the ears; her tail flicks once and her eyes stay on the street. He puts his eye to the gap beside her nose.

Through the link, as soon as he asks, comes her answer. It isn't words, just a feeling: *not food. Not a mouse. Watching.* Under it is the tight, still interest of a cat that hasn't decided whether something is a threat.

Below him the main street is full of morning. Directly across from the Anvil and Ember stands a big smithy with its yard gate wide open. A sign over the arch shows a hammer striking a cloud. A covered wagon is backed up to the gate with two grey mules in harness. A pair of men in plain brown work clothes, with no guild badges, carry pig iron out of the yard two bars at a time and stack it in the wagon bed. Judging by how low the wagon sits on its springs, they've been at it a while.

A woman in a long dust-coloured travelling coat stands by the tailboard with a ledger open on her forearm. She makes a mark for every pair of bars. Beside her, the smith wipes his hands on his apron and doesn't look happy about any of it.

A crow sits on the wagon's canvas, perfectly still.

James lets his eye settle and watches.

He watches for a good while. Mostly what he sees is a load of iron changing hands. Whatever has Penny's attention, he can't catch it. To him the crow is just a crow: black, scruffy, sitting on the canvas the way crows sit on anything. The woman's ledger is too far away to read. The smith says something to her, short and sharp, but the hammers up and down the street drown it out. She answers without looking up from her page.

When the last pair of bars goes in, she shuts the ledger, takes a fat leather purse from inside her coat and counts coins into the smith's palm. It takes a long time. The smith doesn't put the money away. He stands weighing it in his open hand, as if he's still deciding something.

On the canvas the crow hasn't moved a feather. Under James's hand, Penny's back has gone stiff, and her tail is now twitching fast.

Downstairs Marta shouts that the porridge is burning again and that it is *not her fault this time*.

 James squints through the gap until his eye waters, trying to read the scene the way Penny is reading it, and he can't. He can't find whatever she has found. The crow, the wagon, the woman and her purse all look like an ordinary morning sale to him, and the detail that has his cat bristling gets past him.

Penny gives a low, annoyed chirp, as if he's being slow. She doesn't take her eyes off the canvas.

turns.message:
James stops straining his own eye. He rests two fingers on the back of Penny's neck, closes his eyes and drops into the link, looking out through *her* eyes and listening through her ears. His attention goes to the crow on the canvas, not the coins.

"All right, clever girl. Show me."
turns.reply:
James sets two fingers on the warm fur at the back of Penny's neck and closes his eyes. The room drops away. His own body goes dark and quiet, and he is looking out through the shutter gap with the cat's eyes.

The street changes. The morning light is sharper and flatter, and every movement stands out. The hammers are louder too, but Penny's ears pick the noise apart: a clang from the left, a hiss of quenching steel from up the road, mules shifting their hooves. Under all that, faint and in pieces, there are voices at the tailboard.

Then there's the crow.

Seen through Penny's eyes, the crow is plainly wrong. It hasn't preened, shifted its grip on the canvas or so much as glanced at the scraps in the gutter. It's facing the inn with its head cocked, and its eye is fixed on this window, on the gap where a cat's nose is pressed. It's watching Penny, the way Penny is watching it.

James knows that posture. He has seen it on his own cat, every time he rode behind her eyes the way he is doing now. That crow has someone sitting in it.

The voices come through in fragments.

"...third load this tenday," the smith says. He sounds rough and tired. "Silver over the market price on every bar. A man starts wondering, mistress."

"Then don't, Master Fuiruim," she answers, level and dry. "Wonder about something else. The price is the price."

"And if the Fist ever asks me where Beregost iron is going..."

"Tell them you sold it to a buyer who paid in full." The purse strings snap tight. "Same day next tenday. Have it ready."

The crow turns its head, just once, a quick sideways jerk toward the woman.

Without hurrying, she looks up from her purse. She doesn't glance around the street. She looks straight across it at the second floor of the Anvil and Ember, at this window, for the space of a breath. Her face is narrow and sun-browned, and nothing in it changes. Then she looks down again, tucks the ledger under her arm and says something short to her men. They climb onto the wagon bed and start lashing the canvas down. The crow doesn't move, even when the rope passes right beside it. One of the mules tosses its head and stamps, ready to go.

The smith is still in the gateway with her money in his fist, watching the wagon get ready to leave.

Under James's fingers, Penny's whole body has gone tight as a drawn bowstring. Her feeling comes through the link at the same time as the view: *it saw. It TOLD her.*

turns.message:
James breathes out slowly and keeps his fingers on Penny's neck. He stays behind her eyes just long enough to see which way the wagon turns when it pulls out, north toward the Gate or south down the Way toward Nashkel. Then he lets the link go, and Penny backs away from the gap.

He steps back from the window himself, out of the light, and talks low while he pulls on his boots.

"Somebody's sitting in that bird, love, same as I sit in you. And now they know there's a cat at the Anvil and Ember with a man behind her." He buckles on the studded leather, throws the grey cloak over it and hangs Tymora's coin back under his shirt. "Fine. We'll do the open thing, then."

He leaves the purse in his pack, all but a few silver, and goes downstairs. He doesn't stop for breakfast. He heads straight across the street to the smithy gate, where Master Fuiruim is still standing with that woman's money in his fist.

James stops at a polite, unthreatening distance, nods at the hammer-and-cloud sign, and talks like a man with nothing better to do this morning.

"Morning, Master Fuiruim. That's a lot of iron going out the gate before breakfast. And by the look on your face, it's a price you're not happy to be paid." He tilts his head toward the road where the wagon went. "Who's she buying for?"
turns.reply:
James keeps his fingers on Penny's neck and stays behind her eyes.

The labourers pull the last rope tight and climb up front. One of them clicks his tongue at the mules, and the wagon rolls out of the smithy arch with its springs groaning under the load. It doesn't turn north toward the Gate. It swings south onto the Trade Way, toward Nashkel, and joins the morning carts. The woman walks beside the front wheel for a few steps, then pulls herself up onto the bench without looking back.

The crow stays on the canvas until the wagon draws level with the inn. Then it opens its wings, beats once and rises over the street, up past the window close enough that Penny's ears go flat. It circles the roof of the Anvil and Ember once, then turns south after the wagon and stays low over the road.

James lets go. The room comes back: cold floor, the smell of porridge, his own heartbeat. Penny drops off the sill without a sound, gives herself a hard, offended shake and sits in the middle of the floor watching him dress. When he hangs the coin under his shirt, her tail gives one flick. It feels like approval.

Downstairs, Marta Holloway shouts "Breakfast's—" at his back as he walks out without stopping. Then she sighs heavily, loud enough to carry, about men who pay for porridge and don't eat it. Penny pads out after him and sits on the inn step, tucks her paws in and looks bored.

Master Fuiruim hasn't moved from the gateway. Up close he's a big, grey-bearded man with burn-scarred forearms and a leather apron shiny with wear. His fist is still closed around the money. When James speaks, the smith's eyes go to him, then to the cloak, then the coin-bulge under the shirt, the boots, and back to his face. It's how a man looks over a horse he isn't sure he wants to buy.

"Who's asking?" he says. Then, almost against his will, he glances south down the road where the dust of the wagon is settling.

James keeps his voice easy and his hands where the smith can see them. He's a stranger asking about another man's trade, but this man has plainly been wanting to tell someone all morning.

The smith is quiet for a long moment. Then he snorts through his beard, and his shoulders drop. He's been carrying this alone and is tired of it.

"You're not Fist," he says. "Fist would have come with two more and a clerk." He jerks his chin at the empty gateway. "She calls herself Mistress Orrin. First time she came was eight days ago. Didn't haggle and paid in advance, which nobody does. Three loads since. Pig iron, all of it, the best I had, and she wanted it fast. Not tools, not blades, not horseshoes. Just the raw metal."

He looks south again.

"That's what sits wrong. Nashkel's got iron mines of its own, two days nearer than here. So why does anybody haul Beregost bars south, past Nashkel's own ore, unless they don't want Nashkel knowing they're buying?" He shakes his head. "And her men. No badges, no guild. Never a word. Never stop for an ale. I've known Amnian mule-drivers who'd talk to a fencepost."

Then, slowly, he opens his fist.

Most of what's in his palm is honest money, good gold of the Gate and Amn. But four of the coins aren't. They're thicker than a gold piece and not quite round, and worn almost smooth. On one face is a bearded head, so rubbed down that only the line of a crown is left. On the other is a ring of angular letters. They look a little like dwarvish runes, but James has seen dwarvish on enough tomb doors to know they're not. Dark earth is packed hard into the grooves of the letters.

"She paid part of the first load in these too," Fuiruim says quietly. "Gold's gold, weighed out fair, so I took it. The moneychanger at the market wouldn't touch them. Said he'd never seen the mint and didn't want to." He turns one over with a thick thumb. "That's money that's been in the ground, friend. A long time."

He closes his hand again and fixes James with a hard look, narrowed and warier now.

"So. A man walks out of the Anvil and Ember without his breakfast and asks me who she's buying for. What's it to you?"

turns.message:
James lets the question sit a moment and doesn't dress it up.

"Fair question. Truth is, my cat didn't like her crow." He nods up at the inn window, where Penny now sits on the step licking a paw as if none of this concerns her. "That bird never preened once. It watched my window the whole time, and when it turned its head she looked straight up at me. Somebody was riding in it, Master Fuiruim. I know how that's done, because I do it myself." He lets that land, then shrugs. "So now she knows my face, and I'd like to know hers. That's all it is to me. That, and I've buried friends who went into the Nashkel mines and never came out, so iron going south quietly makes the back of my neck itch."

He looks at the closed fist, not greedily, just interested.

"The moneychanger won't take those four. I will, at a fair weight in good Gate gold, and you'll be shot of money you don't trust." He reaches slowly into his belt pouch for silver and gold and holds his other palm out, open. "Let me have a proper look at one first. If I know the mint, I'll tell you for nothing."
turns.reply:
James lets the question sit for a breath before he answers. Fuiruim hears him out with his arms folded and his weight back on his heels. When James gets to the bird that never preened, the smith's eyes go past him to the inn step, where Penny is washing behind one ear and pointedly ignoring both of them.

"Rides it," Fuiruim says flatly. "Like a horse."

He looks at James a while longer, the same way he looked at him before, but slower this time. The Nashkel mines get a small grunt and nothing else; up and down the Way, everybody has buried somebody who went into those shafts. Then he looks at the open palm James is holding out. He snorts through his beard, picks one coin out of the honest gold and drops it there.

"Have your look."

It's heavy, heavier than it ought to be for its size. The edge isn't milled and isn't even round. The coin was cast, not struck: there's a faint seam where two halves of a mould met, all but worn away. James tilts it toward the morning light and runs his thumbnail along the ring of letters. He's seen a lot of old metal in his time: southern tombs, collapsed shrines in the Tethyrian hills, a dragon's leavings that turned out to be mostly brass.

It comes to him all at once, the way old things sometimes do.

He has held a coin like this before, twelve years ago in the Tethyrian hills during the war. His scout troop sheltered from the rain in a barrow, and the dead inside had these on their eyes: the same mould seam, the same heavy cast gold, the same crowned and bearded face. The old sergeant who pocketed them wouldn't spend them. He called them *under-hill gold*. He said they were older than any crown in Tethyr or Amn, left by men who learned their letters from the dwarves and later followed the dwarves into the ground. Nobody in that troop knew what became of those people. The sergeant didn't either.

Now that he's looking for it, James can see why the letters aren't dwarvish. The strokes are Dethek, cut the way a dwarf cuts them, but they don't make dwarvish words. Read as Dwarvish they're nonsense. Somebody used dwarven letters to write a language of their own.

He sees three more things the smith and the moneychanger missed.

First, the earth packed into the letters isn't forest loam or field dirt. It's grey and gritty and fine as flour, with flecks that catch the light: the rock dust that cakes a miner's boots a long way down. It's laced with rust-red that comes off on his thumbnail. This coin lay against iron for a long time, and the iron was old enough to rot.

Second, there's a mark on the reverse, inside the ring of letters, small enough to hide under a fingertip. It was punched into the metal after casting: a circle with a single straight bar through it. Whatever it is, it isn't part of the coin's design. Someone added it later, the way an assayer marks good metal or a temple marks what belongs to it. He doesn't know the sign.

Third, the coin is cold. That shouldn't matter, since it's morning and metal holds the night's chill. But he has been holding it for some time now, it hasn't warmed in his palm at all, and his hand is starting to ache faintly at the bones.

Across the street, Penny has stopped washing. She sits up on the inn step, ears forward, looking at his hand.

Fuiruim has been watching James's face, not the coin. He's seen it change.

"You know it," he says. It's not a question. "Well? And if we deal on the other three, we weigh them at Hendak's scale in the market, in front of people. I'll not have it said Fuiruim passed bad gold to a stranger at his own gate."

---

James turns the coin over once more, then sets it back in Fuiruim's palm instead of holding it. He flexes his fingers against the ache in the bones.

"I know the *kind*," he says quietly. "Not the mint. Nobody does, I think. Saw these in a barrow in the Tethyrian hills, on dead men's eyes. My old sergeant called it under-hill gold. Older than Amn, older than any crown down south. Folk who wrote with dwarf letters and then followed the dwarves into the ground." He taps the grit packed in the runes without touching the coin itself. "And that isn't field dirt. That's deep-shaft dust, and the red in it is rust off old iron. These came up out of a mine, Master Fuiruim, and not long ago."

He points at the little circle with the bar through it. "That mark was punched in after. Somebody's claimed them. You ever seen that sign on anything else? On her wagon, her ledger, a ring on her men?"

He wipes his palm on his cloak like a man brushing off frost.

"Hendak's scale is fair by me. Weighed in front of people, in good Gate gold. My purse is across the street. Give me the time it takes to climb the stairs." He holds the smith's eye a beat longer. "And a word for nothing, soldier to smith: don't keep those by your bed tonight. That one's cold, and it stays cold in a warm hand. Gold doesn't do that."

He glances over at the inn step. Penny is already on her feet.

record.opening: Morning finds you the way luck sometimes does — without asking permission. Grey light slips through the shutters of your room above the Copper Anvil, and Beregost is already awake: hammers ringing from the forges down the street, a carter swearing at his mule, the distant bells of Lathander's temple calling the faithful to greet the dawn. The cat is sitting on the windowsill, tail curled around its paws, watching you with the patient air of a creature who has been awake for hours and wants you to know it. Your purse is heavy — around three hundred and fifty gold from that last hand, the last hand. Your gear is where you left it. From below drifts the smell of fresh bread and the voice of Marta Holloway, the innkeeper, announcing to the whole common room that porridge waits for no one. Nobody expects you anywhere. No job, no debt due, no road you must take before nightfall. And yet, just inside the door, lying face down on the floorboards, is a single playing card. You don't remember it being there last night. The cat has noticed it too — its eyes have gone from you to the card and back again. The day is yours. What do you do?

turns.message:
I sit up and look at the cat first. "Don't give me that face. You were by the door all night, you'd have seen who came in."

Before I touch the card, I reach for my pack and check my own deck in its leather case — is it still full, fifty-two, or is one missing? Then I pick the card up off the floor and turn it over.
turns.reply:
James sits up. The cat holds his stare a moment longer, then blinks, slowly, the way cats do when they're being generous.

The answer comes the way it always does, less a voice than a feeling set down behind his eyes: *Not by the door. The window. It was warm there.* Then a picture to go with it. The room in the dark, seen from the sill. Soft steps in the corridor, someone walking carefully. The steps stop outside. There's a whisper of paper on wood, and something white slides under the door. The steps go away. A smell drifts through the gap: cloves, and the kind of soap you don't buy in Beregost.

Then, with no shame at all: *They didn't come in. You were snoring.*

The pack is where he left it, at the foot of the bed. The leather case is in the inner pocket. Inside is his old deck: blue backs worn soft, corners rounded from years of shuffling in other men's tents. He counts it on the blanket out of habit, quickly and without looking at the faces. Fifty-two. Nothing missing. The cards feel right in his hands, and that's a problem of its own.

He picks the card up off the floor.

It isn't his, and it isn't cheap. The card is stiff and new, with gilt edges, and the back is deep green with a fine pattern of linked keys. When he turns it over it's the Lady of Coins: a crowned woman holding up a single gold coin, painted with real skill. Under her feet someone has written in a neat hand that takes its time:

*Feldepost's. The upper room. Eleventh bell tonight. Bring the purse.*

There's no name and no seal.

James knows this custom. You don't learn it in Beregost. You learn it further south, in Athkatla and in the counting-houses of Zazesspur, where the big private tables never send letters. They slip a card under your door. The suit tells you what's on the table, and Coins means gold and nothing else. The rank tells you how deep the game runs. Nobody hands out a Lady to a man they expect to bet copper.

So someone in this town knows he's carrying money. And someone knows he plays, or used to.

Downstairs Marta Holloway is telling the common room for the second time that porridge waits for no one, and that this means *you, Garrick*. On the sill, Penny has curled her tail back around her paws and is watching the card in James's hand.

 *(Out of game: neither action needed a roll, and both were played last turn. Talking to Penny isn't a check, so she answered: she was on the windowsill, and she gave you the picture of who came to the door. Counting your own deck has no real uncertainty and nothing riding on it, so James just did it: all fifty-two cards are there and none is missing.)*

turns.message:
I put my own deck back in its case and the case back in the pack — deep, under the hardtack, where it takes two hands to reach. The Lady of Coins goes into the fold with my regimental papers. I thumb the coin of Tymora on its cord once, out of habit, and say under my breath, "I didn't ask for that one, Lady. Just so we're clear."

Then I dress, strap on the rod and the cloak, and go down to the common room for porridge. Penny can come or sulk, her choice. While Marta's dishing it out I keep it easy and neighbourly: "Marta — Feldepost's. That the big inn up the road? What sort of house is it? And did anyone come asking after me last night, or after a Tethyrian?"
turns.reply:
James puts the old deck back in its case and pushes the case deep into the pack, under the hardtack and the coil of rope, where it takes both hands and a bit of digging to reach. The gilt card goes into the oilcloth fold with the regimental pay slip, the green back with its linked keys pressed against Zaranda's seal. He thumbs the silver coin on its cord and says what he has to say to the Lady.

Nothing answers. The coin is cool and smells faintly of his own skin, the way it does most mornings.

Penny watches him dress: studded leather, the old regimental cloak, the rod hung at his hip. When he opens the door she gets up, stretches front and back without hurrying, and pads out ahead of him as if going down was her idea. *Kitchen's warm,* comes the thought, and nothing more.

The common room of the Copper Anvil is low and smoky and full. A dozen smiths' apprentices crowd the long table, there are two carters by the window, and an old dwarf eats in silence with his beard tucked into his collar. Penny goes straight to the hearth and takes the best spot on the stones, between a dozing dog and the fire. The dog opens one eye, thinks it over, and shuts it again.

Marta Holloway comes round with the pot on her hip and drops a bowl in front of James without asking. She's up to her elbows in flour and she isn't quiet.

"Porridge comes with the room. Honey's extra and Garrick's had most of it." She ladles, hears him out, and her eyebrows go up at *Feldepost's*.

"Up the road past the smithy with the green sign, aye. Glass in every window and they'll charge you for looking through it. Merchants stay there, folk with their own servants. Lately it's Amnians, factors come up from the south buying iron by the cartload. The smiths love them. I don't. They never eat here." She sniffs. "Nice house. Clean. Quiet, if you like that."

On his other question she stops with the ladle in the air.

"Asking after you? Not at my counter, love, and I'd have remembered a man asking for a Tethyrian." Then she narrows her eyes. "Why? Someone come up my stairs in the night?"

She doesn't wait for an answer. She turns and shouts toward the yard door: "*Tam!*" Nobody comes. She turns back, and she's annoyed now, not at James.

"I bar the front at midnight. The yard door's Tam's. He's my stable lad, fifteen, freckles, and a mouth that never stops. He was up Feldepost's way yesterday evening taking back a lamed horse for one of their guests. He came home whistling with a silver piece in his pocket. Told me he'd found it." She sets the pot down hard on the table. "He carried your pack up, didn't he? And saw you pay for the room in gold."

She looks at James a moment longer, and under the noise she's sharp and curious, and she minds about her house.

"He's out the back mucking out the stalls, if you want a word. Now. Are you in some kind of trouble I ought to know about?"
