turns.message:
James listens to it all without interrupting. When Garrick takes the sword back onto his knees, he nods once.

"Fair. Turning back is yours and Quell's. Stopping is mine. That's a split I can live with." He scoops the silver and copper off the table into his purse. "And I'll settle the money with Quell myself, like you say."

He stands and stretches until his back cracks, then glances down at the water cup under Garrick's hand.

"One thing, Sergeant, and then I'll leave it. I made my living for ten years watching men's hands across a table. Yours goes to that cup every time you talk about the men who didn't come back, and it stays there." He says it lightly, without any edge. "Maybe that's grief. I've seen that tell on honest men too. But if one of those seven guards was yours, or you sent somebody on that run who shouldn't have gone, I'd rather hear it from you on the road than work it out at the ford."

He doesn't wait for an answer. He swings the cloak straight on his shoulders.

"We'll go now, before the second bell. I'd like to see the yard while it's just Ambry and the loaders, before the man paying for it walks in and everyone stands up straighter."

He clicks his tongue softly toward the hearth. *Come on, your ladyship. Work.* On the way to the door he catches Tobin's eye across the room and gives him a small nod that says *keep watching*.

*(Out of game: if Garrick's answer about the cup is something James would read with Insight, I'll roll it. I'm not proficient, so it's Wisdom +1.)*
turns.reply:
Garrick doesn't move while James talks. The hand on the cup stays where it is. He doesn't pull it away when it's named either, and that tells James something by itself. He just looks at it, as if it belonged to another man.

James watches him for the answer under the answer, the way he used to watch a man deciding whether to call. He doesn't get it. Garrick's face goes still and stays like that, a sergeant's face on parade, and whatever is behind it stays there. It might be grief, guilt, or just an old soldier who doesn't like being read in a common room. From across a breakfast table James can't tell which, and it bothers him a little that he can't.

Garrick takes his hand off the cup and lays it flat on the table beside the other.

"On the road," he says. That's all. It isn't a yes, and it isn't a denial.

He plants his right boot, gets the stiff leg out from under the table and stands. The sword goes onto his belt properly this time, the buckle drawn tight with a tug. He looks at the cup once more before he leaves it.

"Now suits. Ambry'll be at the gate by this hour. Quell keeps a strict book, and the boy keeps it stricter."

By the hearth there's a small scrape of claws on stone. The cat comes out from among the ash buckets, stops to stretch one back leg as if it were her own idea, and pads after James. She goes past Garrick's boots close enough to brush them. He looks down at her, then at James, and says nothing about it.

Tobin is wiping a table that doesn't need wiping. He catches the nod and gives a very serious one back, and then he can't help glancing at the door where the grey horse stands.

Outside, Beregost is fully awake. Hammers ring up and down the street out of time with each other. Coal smoke hangs low over the roofs, and a cart of charcoal is backing into a forge yard with a great deal of advice from both ends. Garrick unties the grey. The saddlebags are still buckled the way they were, and Tobin has done his job. Garrick leads the horse by the bridle instead of riding. They walk south down the Way together, the old sergeant's uneven step beside James's silent one, and the cat runs ahead along the edge of a water trough.

The chandler's is a narrow shop smelling of tallow, with bundles of dipped candles hung in the window like onions. Behind it a gate of grey planks stands half open in a yard wall. It's a quarter of an hour's walk from the inn.

Inside, the yard is beaten earth with a long shed down one side. Three wagons stand in a row under the shed roof with their tilts rolled back. Two are loaded nearly to the boards and the third is half done. A pair of men are swinging small casks up into it, salt by the white crust on the staves. Beside the gate, at a trestle with a ledger open on it and a stone on each page against the wind, stands a thin young man of about twenty. He has ink on two fingers and a pen behind his ear. He looks up at the horse, then at Garrick, and then at James and his cloak. He looks longest at the cat, who has already jumped onto the end of the trestle and sat down on the corner of his ledger.

"Sergeant." He puts a finger on the page as if the cat might carry it off. "Master Quell's not in till the second bell. Is this—" He stops, and doesn't quite know how to finish.

"The scout," Garrick says. "Master Worgen. He wants to see the wagons, the load and the men. Show him what he asks for, Ambry."

The two loaders have stopped with a cask between them and are watching.

 *(Out of game: I'll spell the Insight check out more plainly. I don't want it to read as a reaction.)*

James set out to read Sergeant Venn and couldn't. He looked for the small giveaways a card player waits for: the jaw tightening, the blink coming too late, the eyes going somewhere they shouldn't. Garrick showed none of them. He'd spent thirty years standing still while officers shouted in his face, and his face gave nothing away. James walked out of the Anvil and Ember knowing no more than when he sat down. The hand stays on the cup, the man keeps quiet, and one of the seven might have been his, or might not.
changes: Insight (Wisdom +1, not proficient): reading Garrick's face when the cup is named: 9 vs 15 — failure
Promise kept: Tobin watches the grey horse
Journal: “Scout for Quell's caravan to Nashkel” updated

turns.message:
James scoops the cat off the ledger before she can sit on anything important. He drapes her over his shoulder, where she settles with an offended flick of the tail.

"My apologies, Master Ambry. She thinks every book is a bed." He gives the clerk an easy smile and keeps his voice friendly, not an officer's. "I won't keep you long. A strict book is exactly what I came to see."

He nods at the open ledger without touching it.

"Show me the page for the last run, the one that never reached Nashkel. Who drove and who guarded, what was loaded, and when the date was set. Then show me tomorrow's. And if you keep note of it, I'd like to know who came asking about either date: the factor's letter, the chandler, the cooper, anyone. Even someone who just stopped at the gate to chat about when Quell's wagons go south." He lowers his voice a little. "Especially them."

He turns slightly as he speaks, so he can watch the two loaders with their cask from the corner of his eye. He wants to see whether they go back to work, keep listening, or look at each other.

At the same time he sends a quiet thought to the warm weight on his shoulder: *In a minute, go down and have a sniff round the wagons. Wheels, axles, under the boards. Anything that isn't salt, oil or cloth.* He won't look through her eyes yet. He wants his own on the clerk and the loaders.

record.opening: Grey morning light slips through the shutters of a small room above the Bellows Inn. Out in the street Beregost is already at work: hammers ring from the smithies, a cart rattles along the Trade Way, and somewhere east the temple of Lathander greets the dawn with a bell. The purse is still there, heavy with about three hundred and fifty gold from the last hand you will ever win. The goddess saw to that, and she saw to the terms. Your cat sits on the windowsill, tail curled, watching the street with the patience of a creature that owes no one anything. Fresh bread and frying bacon drift up through the floorboards, along with the voice of the innkeeper, Marta Hollin, calling orders to the kitchen. Then a second voice, a man's, low and unhurried, one you do not know: "The Tethyrian. He still upstairs?" A pause. The scrape of a chair. The cat's ears turn toward the door. The day is yours, and for the moment no one has told you what to do with it.

turns.message:
I'm awake before the chair finishes scraping. Old habit: boots first, then the studded leather, cloak over it, rod into my belt, the coin on its cord under my shirt. I don't hurry, but I don't waste a motion either.

*To the cat, through the bond:* "Go down. Quietly. Have a look at the man asking after Tethyrians — how he's dressed, what he's carrying, whether he's alone. Don't let him pay you any mind."

I crack the door for the cat and let it slip out ahead of me, then stay by the door with my ear to the gap, listening to Marta's answer and whatever comes next, while I finish buckling the quiver to my belt.
turns.reply:
The chair downstairs finishes its scrape. By then the boots are on, and the studded leather settles over your shoulders. The faded regimental cloak goes over the leather, the rod goes through your belt, and the Lady's coin drops cool against your breastbone under the shirt. The soldier's habits are all still there.

The cat is off the sill before you finish the thought. It pours through the gap in the door, drops down the stairs one step at a time with its tail up, the picture of a house cat that wants bacon, and is gone round the banister.

You stay at the gap. Marta Hollin's voice carries the way an innkeeper's voice has to.

"He is. Paid through tomorrow, and he's not to be dragged out of bed by anyone who hasn't bought breakfast." A plate goes down on wood. "Sit. You look like the road chewed you and spat you back."

"I'll sit." It's the low voice again, unhurried. He has no need to be loud. "Whatever's hot. When he comes down, tell him Brandt would like a word. It's work. Paid work."

"Pell's been telling the whole street about your Tethyrian, has he."

"Pell said he'd soldiered. Said you can see it in how he sits at a table." A pause. "Is it true?"

"I don't ask my guests their trade, Master Brandt. I ask them for silver." She raises her voice toward the kitchen: "*Two eggs, bacon, the dark bread!*"

The pictures come up the bond the way a cat sends them. They're mostly smell and shape, all crowded together.

Horse, strongly. Old sweat and road mud, dried to the knee on heavy boots. Under that, faint and sharp, blood, and it's fresh. The cat has it placed: a clean linen bandage round his left forearm, under a rolled sleeve.

The man is in his forties, big through the shoulders, with grey in a short beard. A brown road coat hangs open over a mail shirt that has seen rain. He has a plain-hilted longsword with the grip worn dark, and a long knife at the hip. A leather satchel sits on the bench beside him, buckled shut. He has taken the corner table with his back to the wall, facing the foot of the stairs. Nobody sits with him. Two carters by the hearth glance his way once and go back to their porridge.

Then the cat's attention snags on something, the way it would on a moth. On the table, by his good hand, lies a crossbow bolt. It's short and thick, fletched with black feathers. The head isn't the grey of iron. It's darker, almost bluish, like something left too long in a forge's quench. He isn't looking at it. Now and then his thumb rolls it a quarter-turn on the boards.

The cat sits down under the next table and washes a paw. Brandt looks at it once and pays it no more mind.

Marta comes out with his plate. "Eat. He'll come down when he comes down."

"I'll be here," Brandt says, and picks up his fork with his left hand. Something about the bandage makes him wince, and he swaps the fork to the other hand.
changes: Hal Brandt now has: Black-fletched crossbow bolt

turns.message:
I let the door close soft behind me and come down the stairs the ordinary way — not creeping, not stamping. A man who's been told there's work waiting doesn't need to hide that he's heard it.

At the foot of the stairs I catch Marta's eye first. "Morning, Mistress Hollin. Whatever he's having, and a mug of something hot." A silver piece goes on the counter for it.

Then I cross to the corner table and stop a pace short of it, hands easy and in view, the way you approach a man who's chosen the wall at his back.

"Brandt. I'm the Tethyrian Pell's been so free with." I nod at the bandage, then at the bolt under his thumb. "That one's not from a Fist armoury. Mind if I sit, or do you want to eat first?"
turns.reply:
Your purse holds only gold, so the coin you put on the counter is a gold piece. Marta takes it, counts nine silver back into your palm and doesn't look up.

"Same as him, then." She's already turning to the kitchen hatch. "And the kettle's on. Find a seat."

The common room is low-beamed and warm, with a fire going in the hearth. The two carters by the hearth watch you cross, decide you're none of their business and go back to their porridge. Under the next table the cat stops washing and settles with its paws tucked in. It's close enough to your boot to lean on it if it wanted to. It doesn't.

Brandt watches you all the way from the stairs. He doesn't stand. His eyes go to your hands, then the rod in your belt, then the cloak. They stay on the cloak a moment longer. When you stop a pace short of the table, he puts his fork down.

He hears out what you say about the bolt without looking at it. His thumb stays where it is.

"No," he says. "It's not."

Up close you see it's a heavy-crossbow quarrel, thicker and shorter than the bolts in your own case, built to punch through mail. Twelve years of war in Tethyr and the road after it put a lot of other men's ammunition through your hands: Amnian, Calishite, Zhentarim, and plenty of plain blacksmith's work from the villages. None of it looked like this. The head isn't rusted, it isn't pitted and it isn't polished. It's just dark all the way through. Someone shaped it with care.

"Sit," Brandt says. He nods at the bench across from him, the one that puts your back to the room, and doesn't apologise for it. "I can eat and talk."

He waits until you're down. Then he says it straight, the way a man lays out a route.

"Six wagons. Iron and wool out of Nashkel, bound for the Gate. We roll north at first light tomorrow. Four days, if the weather holds. I had six blades. I've got four." He touches the bandage once, briefly, as if to check it's still there. "Three gold a day, your food, and a place by the fire. Paid at the Gate."

He picks the fork back up in his right hand and doesn't eat yet.

"Pell says you soldiered. Says he can see it in how you sit." He looks at the cloak again, at the faded regimental colour. "Where?"

 Out of game: none of these three needed a roll, because nothing about them was uncertain, and all three happened in the last turn. You paid Marta a gold piece and got nine silver back. You crossed the room and stopped a pace short of Brandt's table with your hands in view. You greeted him, nodded at the bandage and the bolt, and asked whether you could sit. He answered: "No. It's not," about the bolt, and then "Sit." One correction to the list: as I read your order, "whatever he's having" was breakfast for James, not food for Brandt, and that's how I played it. If you meant to buy Brandt's meal, say so and I'll fix it. The turn ended on Brandt's question, "Where?", which is waiting for your answer.
changes: −1 gp (Paid Marta Hollin a gold piece for breakfast and a hot drink)
+9 sps (Nine silver in change from Marta for the gold piece (breakfast cost 1 sp))

turns.message:
I sit. Back to the room — I've sat worse places. The cat shifts so its flank rests against my boot after all, and I let it.

"Tethyr. Zaranda's foot, then her scouts, from the siege of Zazesspur till the crown was on her head. Twelve years on and off, counting the companies after." I don't dress it up; a man like Brandt will hear the names and know what they cost. "I can hit a man at a hundred paces and I don't panic when the line breaks. Close in, I'm a worse bargain. I'll tell you that now so you don't find it out on the road."

I turn my mug when Marta sets it down, let the heat into my hands, and nod at the bandage again.

"You had six. Now you've four, and one of them's eating with the wrong hand. Before I say yes to three gold a day and a wagon bound for the Gate — what happened to the other two, and where were you when that thing" — the bolt — "went looking for your arm?"
turns.reply:
Brandt watches you take the bench. Your back is to the room now, and he doesn't comment on it. Under the table the cat settles its weight against your boot.

He hears the names without moving. At *Zazesspur* his eyes come up from his plate and stay on you. When you tell him you're a worse bargain close in, one corner of his mouth shifts. It isn't quite a smile.

"Most men tell me what they're good at," he says. "Not many tell me the other half."

Marta comes past and puts the mug down by your hand, and a plate after it: two eggs, bacon still spitting, a heel of dark bread. She's back at the kitchen hatch before either of you looks up.

Brandt eats a little before he answers. When he does, he lays it out in order, the way a man gives a report he has already given once and didn't like giving.

"Two nights ago. Half a day south of here, toward Nashkel. We camped off the road, wagons in a ring, two men on watch and the fire low. Proper." He sets the fork down. "They came after midnight. No horns, no shouting. The first I knew of it was a man screaming at the far side of the ring, then nothing. It was dark. I counted six of them, maybe eight. They moved like they'd done it before."

He touches the bandage.

"That was a knife. One of them got in close while I was getting my sword clear. Never saw his face. He wore something over it." His thumb finds the bolt and gives it its quarter-turn. "This one went into the wagon board a hand from my head. There were more. They didn't loose many. They didn't need to."

"Corran and Wil had the watch. Corran's been with me nine years. Wil's nineteen." His voice stays level. "They took them both, and the third wagon with its team. There was blood where Corran stood, not much. No bodies. Not that night, not in the morning."

He looks at you then, straight.

"The third wagon carried iron. Pig iron out of Nashkel. The strongbox was under the seat of the second wagon, ten feet away, with the merchants' coin in it. They walked past it." He lets that sit a moment. "Bandits take the coin."

He picks the fork up again in his right hand and doesn't use it.

"At first light I followed the wheel ruts west off the road, toward the trees. I lost them on stony ground after a mile, maybe two. Then I had a choice to make. I had five wagons, three merchants and three men who could still hold a sword, standing in the open. I turned back." He doesn't explain it any further. "One of my three went home here in Beregost yesterday, and I don't blame him. That's why I've got four, counting me."

He finally takes a bite of egg and chews it, his eyes still on you.

"That's all of it, as far as I know it. You asked where I was. I was at the wagons." A pause. "You looked at that bolt like you know bolts. What do you see?"

 Out of game: neither of these needed a roll, because nothing about them was uncertain, and both happened last turn. You sat on the bench with your back to the room, and the cat leaned against your boot. You asked about the two missing guards and where Brandt was, and he told you plainly. Corran and Wil were on watch and were taken with the iron wagon. He was at the wagons, where a knife cut his arm and the bolt hit the board beside his head. The turn ended on his question to you: "What do you see?" in the bolt.

turns.message:
I hold out my hand, palm up, for the bolt rather than just taking it. When he lets me, I turn it in the light from the hearth — the fletching, the way the shaft's been trimmed, the head most of all. I run a thumbnail along the edge of it and tilt it to see whether the dark goes all the way through or sits on the surface like a bluing.

"I've had Amnian quarrels pulled out of men, and Calishite, and Zhentarim, and village work that was barely more than a nail on a stick. None of them looked like this." I say it quietly, thinking aloud for him. "This is smith's work, and a smith who cared. Heavy crossbow — a weapon for a wall or a wagon-bed, not a man running through the dark. Black fletching and a head that doesn't catch the light. Someone built these for the night, Brandt. That's not six lads who turned bandit after the harvest failed."

I set it back down by his hand, head toward him.

"They walked past the strongbox and took the iron and two men who could lift it. That's cargo, not plunder. Somebody's smelting or forging and doesn't want to buy at the Beregost price." I hold his eye. "So before I say yes — who have you told? The Fist? The merchants whose iron it was? And has anyone in this town been asking about iron this past month — buying it, or asking where it goes?"
turns.reply:
Brandt looks at your open hand for a moment. Then he picks up the bolt and puts it in your palm, fletching first.

It's heavier than it looks. The shaft is ash, straight-grained and close-sanded. The black feathers are trimmed low and short, so it will fly quiet and won't whistle. The head is socketed, not tanged, and filed to a narrow four-sided point. When you run your thumbnail down one edge it catches and scrapes, and no bright metal shows under the scratch. The dark isn't bluing or lacquer. It goes all the way through. You tilt it toward the hearth, and the firelight slides over it without catching.

Somewhere in the back of your head, an old habit of the companies' years starts asking what kind of metal turns firelight like that.

You've seen metal like this once before. It was in a wizard's cellar in Myratma, the year one of the companies stripped it of everything that wasn't nailed down. There were ingots on a shelf down there, as dark as this, and they took the hearth's light the same dull way. The company's hedge-mage picked one up and put it straight down again. He called it *ready iron*: metal smelted with something extra in the melt, so it would hold an enchantment later. It was the enchanter's blank. You remember it was cold. This head has been in your palm a good while, a yard from the fire, and it hasn't warmed at all.

Nothing seems to be working in it now, not that you can feel. Either nobody ever put a charm in it, or whatever was in it is gone.

Then the light slides over the socket and you see something else. Just under the rim, where the shaft would hide it, someone has punched a mark into the metal: a ring the size of a lentil with three short strokes inside it, side by side. It's worn, but it was made on purpose. Village smiths don't stamp their bolts. Armouries do, but every army stamp you know is bigger, and they put it where the quartermaster can see it.

You give him your read the way you thought it through, and you lay the bolt down by his hand with the head pointing at him.

Brandt hears you out without moving. When you get to *cargo, not plunder* his jaw sets, as if you've said something he'd already told himself and didn't like hearing again. He takes his time over your questions, one at a time.

"The Fist. Yesterday, at their post by the bridge." He pushes his plate an inch away. "A sergeant wrote it in a book. He said it's the third train since spring between here and Nashkel, and he's got eleven men for the whole road. He was sorry. He meant it. That's all he had to give."

"Three merchants ride with me. The iron was Tobin Hask's, out of Nashkel, sold to a foundry at the Gate and paid for half in advance. Hask knows. He spent yesterday writing letters. He wants it back more than he wants the money, and he won't say why."

He looks at the bolt and doesn't touch it.

"Asking about iron in Beregost, I don't know. It's not my town. You'd want a smith." He goes quiet, and when he speaks again it's slower. "At Nashkel, though. The weighing yard, the morning we loaded. A man asked the weighmaster which wagon the iron went in, and what day we'd roll. I never saw him. The weighmaster told me after, as a joke. Some fellow wanting to know his business, he said."

He lets that sit, then looks straight at you.

"They knew which wagon, Worgen. In the dark, in a ring of six, they went to the third."

His thumb moves toward the bolt and stops short of it.

"That's all I know. You know it now too." He waits a moment. "Is it yes?"

 James's knowledge holds up. Turning the bolt-head in the firelight, he works out what it is for certain: ready iron, a blank smelted to take an enchantment. That's no guess from the colour. He has felt it in his hand once before, and he knows the cold that won't leave it.

*Out of game: the card added +4 for Arcana, but your sheet says +3. That's a 19 instead of a 20 against the 15, so it's a success either way. Brandt's question, "Is it yes?", is still waiting for your answer.*
changes: Arcana: read what's in the bolt-head's dark metal: 20 vs 15 — success
Changed: Black-fletched crossbow bolt (James examined it and recognised the metal as ready iron. He also found a hidden maker's stamp.)
New place: Flaming Fist post, Beregost
A rumour of a place: Nashkel weighing yard
New person: Flaming Fist sergeant (Beregost post)

turns.message:
"It's yes." I say it plainly, and then I pick up my fork, because a man who's just hired on eats his breakfast. "I'm bound for the Gate anyway. Three a day and food, paid at the Gate — agreed. Two things, though, and I'd rather have them now than argue them on the road."

I hold up one finger. "The bolt. Lend it to me for the day. Beregost's a smith's town, and a smith will know a stamp I don't. If someone's buying forge-blanks here, or selling them, the men at the anvils will have heard. I'll have it back to you by sundown."

Second finger. "Hask. I want a word with him before we roll. Not to squeeze him — I don't care what he's hiding from his wife or his creditors. But a man who wants his iron back more than his money knows what the iron's *for*, and I'd like to know that too before I stand watch over the rest of it in the dark." I nod toward the window and the street. "Where's he lodging, and does he know you're hiring?"

Then, quieter, between mouthfuls: "And Brandt — the man at Nashkel who asked which wagon. Did the weighmaster say what he looked like? Even 'ordinary' tells me something."
turns.reply:
Brandt watches you pick up the fork. He doesn't smile, but his shoulders come down a little.

"Good," he says.

He hears out both of your conditions without interrupting. When you hold up the first finger he looks down at the bolt and is quiet for a moment. Then he slides it across the boards to you with two fingers, fletching first, the way he handed it over before.

"It's the only thing they left me," he says. "Sundown."

The ash shaft is still cold against your palm, though it's been lying a yard from the fire.

At the second finger his mouth tightens, though not at you.

"Hask's at Feldepost's, up the street toward the temple. The one with the green door. He's paying a third of your wage, so yes, he knows I'm hiring. He told me to find a soldier." Brandt picks up his bread and tears it in half. "He'll talk to you. Whether he tells you anything is another matter. He's been civil with me for two days and hasn't said one word more than he has to. This morning he'll be down at the post-rider's with his letters, if he isn't back already."

He eats. When you ask about the man at Nashkel, he chews slowly and looks past you at the room while he thinks back.

"The weighmaster thought it was funny. That's why he told me." He swallows. "He said the fellow asked civil and talked like a counting-house clerk. Ink on his fingers. He paid for his cup at the yard with Amnian silver, which in Nashkel tells you nothing. Half the town's paid in it." A pause. "Then he said the man had his boots blacked, in a mining yard. That's what he was laughing at."

He wipes the plate with the last of the bread and pushes it away.

"That's all I have. I never asked more, because at the time I didn't think there was more to ask." He gets up and settles the road coat over the bandaged arm with a small grimace. "I'll be with the wagons in the yard behind this place most of the day. If you want the other three, they're there. We roll at first light, Worgen. Don't come back drunk."

He nods to Marta on his way out, and the back door lets in a breath of cold air and the smell of horse.

Under the table the cat has decided the bacon on your plate is a real possibility. It puts one paw up on your knee.
changes: A rumour of a place: The post-rider's, Beregost
New place: Wagon yard behind the Bellows
Lent: Black-fletched crossbow bolt → James Worgen — Lent by Hal Brandt for the day; James is to return it by sundown
Quest: Guard Brandt's train to Baldur's Gate (reward: 3 gp a day, food and a place by the fire, paid at the Gate. Tobin Hask pays a third of the wage.)
Promise: Return the bolt to Brandt by sundown

turns.message:
A strip of bacon goes under the table without my looking down. The paw comes off my knee. We understand each other.

I finish the eggs, wrap the bolt in a scrap of oilcloth from the component pouch so the head's hidden, and tuck it inside the cloak. Then I take my mug over to the counter where Marta's working.

"Mistress Hollin. I'm in the trade for the day, it seems." I set the mug down. "Beregost's got more anvils than I've got fingers. If a man wanted to know who in this town understands *unusual* iron — not horseshoes, the kind of work a smith would frown at and then ask where you got it — whose door would he knock on? And is there anyone who's been buying up pig iron this past month, or asking after where the Nashkel loads go?"

A second silver finds its way onto the counter beside the mug, for her trouble and her memory.
turns.reply:
The bacon goes under the table. Something down there takes it neatly, and the paw doesn't come back.

The eggs are good. When the plate is clean you take a scrap of oilcloth from the component pouch and wrap the bolt-head until no metal shows. Even through the cloth it's cold. It goes inside the cloak, against the leather, and you take your mug to the counter.

Marta is cutting bread with a knife that has seen a lot of bread. She lets you finish, looks at the silver on the counter and then at you. She doesn't pick it up yet.

"Unusual iron," she says. "In Beregost you can't throw a boot without hitting a smith. Most of them shoe horses and tell you they don't." The knife goes through the loaf. "You want the Thunderhammer. Top of the street, past the temple, on the left. It's the big one with the hammer over the door. Dagny Fuiruim runs it now. Her family's had that forge since before my grandmother. She's rude, she's dear, and nobody on the Way knows more about metal. If she frowns at it she'll tell you why. And if she asks where you got it, tell her the truth, because she'll know when you don't."

She stacks the slices and wipes the knife on her apron.

"Pig iron, I can't say. Not my trade." Then she stops for a moment, the way someone does when they decide a thing isn't really gossip. "I'll tell you what I hear at the tap, though. Every smith who drinks here has been moaning since spring that pig iron's gone dear. They say someone's been buying whole loads off the Nashkel carts before they get into town, cash on the road, and paying over the price. The little forges can't match it. Old Tam Orrin let his boy go over it." She shrugs. "Who's buying, they don't say. Either they don't know or they won't. Dagny would know if anyone does. And she'd be glad to complain about it to a stranger."

Only then does she take the silver. It goes into the apron pocket without a look.

"Master Brandt's a decent man," she says, quieter, and she's already turning back to the bread. "His lads used to eat at that table. Bring him something worth having."

Out in the street a hammer starts up close by, then another farther off, and a third. Somewhere up the hill a fourth joins them, heavier and slower than the rest. It might be the Thunderhammer.

Journal: “The raid on Brandt's train” updated

turns.message:
"Thank you, Mistress. I'll try."

I drink off the mug, settle the cloak so the regimental patch shows — in a smith's town an old soldier gets more patience than a stranger with questions — and head out into the street. The cat comes to the door, considers the mud and the hammers, and follows along the wall-tops and fence rails rather than the gutter.

Up the hill, past the temple of Lathander, following the slow heavy hammer-stroke to the forge with the hammer over the door. I don't march in on a smith at work. I stand a pace inside the open doorway where the heat reaches me, out of the way of the quench and the bellows, and wait for Dagny Fuiruim to finish the heat she's on and look up — the way you wait on a sergeant who's busy.

When she does: "Mistress Fuiruim. I'm told you're the one who knows metal on this road. I've got a piece I'd like you to frown at, and I'll pay for the time. Brandt's caravan — I'm riding north with it tomorrow."

record.opening:
Morning comes to Beregost the way it always does: hammers. The first smith starts before the light is properly up, a second answers him across the street, and soon the whole town is ringing like a forge-yard. Under that sound a temple bell tolls for Lathander's dawn.

You wake in a narrow bed in a rented room above the Anvil and Ember. The shutters let in a thin grey light. Your gear is where you left it, and your purse is heavier than it has been in a long time — about three hundred and fifty gold, the winnings from that last hand. No one is waiting for you. Nothing has to be done today.

The cat is not curled at your feet. It sits on the windowsill, tail wrapped around its paws, ears pricked forward, staring down into the inn yard without blinking. Whatever it is watching, it hasn't moved for a while.

Footsteps come along the corridor. There is a brisk knock, and a young woman's voice calls through the door: "Morning, sir! Porridge and fresh bread downstairs while it's hot — and do you want the room another night? Mother's asking."

The hammers keep ringing. The cat's tail twitches once.

turns.message:
“Breakfast, certainly. Another night depends on your mother’s price,” I call back. “I’ll be down shortly.”

I get out of bed and join the cat at the window, looking down into the yard. “What’s caught your eye, then?”
turns.reply:
The footsteps stop outside the door. "Five silver, same as last night, supper in!" Dela calls through it. "Mother says she'll take four if you're staying the tenday, but don't tell anyone I said so." Then she's off down the corridor, knocking on the next door before you can answer.

The floor is cold under your feet. You cross to the window and lean on the sill beside the cat, and it shifts over a little to make room without taking its eyes off the yard.

Down below, the Anvil and Ember's yard is waking up. The ostler is forking hay into the stalls. A boy is carrying water. Most of the space is taken up by a big four-wheeled freight wagon that wasn't there when you went to bed. It's covered with oiled canvas and lashed down tight, and it sits low on its springs. Where the canvas has slipped at one corner you can see dull grey bars stacked inside: pig iron, a full load of it. Two drivers you don't recognise are leading a pair of draught horses out of the stable towards it, and they don't look like Beregost men. They're too clean, and their boots are too good. A lean man in a grey travelling coat stands by the gate with the innkeeper, counting coins into her palm one at a time.

None of that is what the cat is looking at.

Its voice comes into your head, low and unhurried, the way it always speaks when it's been patient for a long time:

*Under the wagon. Between the back wheels.*

You look. The shadow under the wagon bed is deep, but now that you know where to look you can see a pair of boots in it, heels down in the straw, and the edge of a leather apron. Someone is lying flat on his back under the axle, perfectly still.

*He crawled in before the bell,* the cat says. *He smells of coal smoke and of being frightened. He has not moved since.* Its tail twitches. *The horses are coming.*

In the yard, one of the drivers backs the first horse towards the wagon shafts and starts on the harness buckles.

turns.message:
I call down to the drivers, keeping my eyes off the hiding place. “Hold a moment! Are you bound north? I’m looking for passage towards Baldur’s Gate.”

Through our bond, I ask the cat, *Can you slip down and warn him the wagon’s about to move? Quietly—don’t draw anyone’s attention to him.*
turns.reply:
James pushes the shutter wide and leans out over the sill, eyes on the gate. "Hold a moment! Are you bound north? I'm looking for passage towards Baldur's Gate."

The driver at the shafts looks up with a buckle in his hand. He's broad, his beard is trimmed, and the morning's hay hasn't touched him. "North, aye, only as far as the—"

"Not as far as the Gate." The man in the grey coat doesn't raise his voice, and it carries anyway. He puts the last coin into Mistress Hartwick's palm and closes her fingers over it before he turns to the window. His face is narrow and shaved close, and he looks polite and tired. "We don't take passengers, I'm afraid. The Gate caravans make up at Feldepost's, at the north end of the street. They'll have a seat for you." He nods once, as if that settles it. The driver goes back to his buckle without another word.

While their eyes are on the window, the cat has already gone. It drops from the sill on the far side of the frame onto the stable roof below.

The cat runs along the stable roof, drops behind the water butt and crosses the straw in three low, unhurried strides. The ostler forks hay right past it and never looks down. Nobody in the yard turns. A moment later the cat is in the dark under the wagon bed.

Through the bond you see what it sees: a young face, sixteen at most, smudged with soot under a tangle of brown hair. He's lying on his back with both arms hooked over the rear axle. A leather strap is looped around the axle and buckled across his chest, and his boots are braced against the crossbar. When the cat's eyes meet his he startles hard, then catches himself and doesn't move. His lips barely shape the words.

"Go on. *Get.* Go away."

The cat sits down in the straw beside his shoulder.

*He cannot hear me,* it tells you. *But he knows the horses are coming. He tied himself on.* A pause. *He is not hiding from the wagon. He is going with it.*

In the yard, the first horse stands in the shafts. The second driver leads the other one round to its place. In the gateway the man in grey pulls on his gloves, one finger at a time.

turns.message:
“Feldepost’s, then. My thanks.” I step back from the window.

*Come back safely,* I tell the cat. *His choice—but I’d like to know why he’s making it.*

I pull on my boots, gather my gear and head downstairs to find Mistress Hartwick. “Morning. That iron wagon—local smiths making a delivery, or traders passing through?”
turns.reply:
James steps back from the window and lets the shutter swing half to.

*Come back safely,* he tells the cat. *His choice. But I'd like to know why he's making it.*

Through the bond he feels the cat take that in without comment. He sits on the bed to pull on his boots, buckles the studded leather, settles the old regimental cloak on his shoulders and slings the crossbow. While he works, the yard sounds come up through the floor: a harness chain jingling, a man clicking his tongue at a horse, the ostler saying something and getting no answer.

The stairs creak under him all the way down. The common room smells of oat porridge and new bread. Two smiths in scorched aprons sit at a bench with their bowls, eating fast before the forges need them. Mistress Hartwick isn't behind the counter. The yard door is propped open, and James finds her just outside it with her arms folded. She is a broad, grey-haired woman with flour on one sleeve, and she is watching the gate.

The iron wagon is rolling. The springs groan under the load, and the wheels grind through the straw and out onto the street. The bearded driver is up on the box with the reins. The other one walks at the lead horse's head. The man in grey rides behind on a neat dun mare and doesn't look back. At the gate the wagon swings left, north up the main street, and the canvas sways as it turns.

A small dark shape drops off the back axle-tree just before the wheels clear the gateway. It lands in the straw and trots back across the yard as if it had business elsewhere.

*He let me go,* the cat says. It comes to sit by James's boot and starts licking one paw. *He has a hammer in the front of his apron. He was holding it the whole time.* The wagon's rumble fades up the street, under the hammering. *They turned towards the north end.*

Mistress Hartwick unfolds her arms and gives James a once-over, boots to cloak. "Morning. You'll be the one who shouted out the window." She doesn't seem annoyed about it. "Those? Traders passing through. Not smiths, and they've never once said they were. That's their third load since the thaw. They buy off Taerom's mostly, and Bram Ironside's, and anybody else with pig to sell." She opens her hand. Four gold coins lie in her palm. They're heavier and brighter than Beregost money, and each one is stamped with a crowned tower. "Pays in Amnian danters, and he's never haggled over a copper. Not the iron and not my rooms." She shuts her hand and slips the coins into her apron. "Half the street thanks Lathander for them, and the other half won't say anything at all. Taerom Fuiruim's been like a bear with a sore tooth since the last load went out. Something to do with one of his lads, but you'd have to ask him, because he doesn't talk to me about it."

She turns back to the doorway, then stops.

"Dela said she asked you about the room. Five silver with supper, or four a night if you're staying the tenday. Which is it?"

Travel: The Anvil and Ember — inn yard (6 minutes)

turns.message:
“One more night.” I count out five silver. “And a piece of bread for the road, if you please.”

I lower my voice. “There was a lad in a smith’s apron strapped beneath that wagon. Alive, hiding deliberately. I tried to delay them before I realised he meant to go along. Where can I find Taerom? If that’s his apprentice, he ought to know now.”
turns.reply:
Your purse turns up nothing but gold. You put one gold piece on the doorframe ledge, and Mistress Hartwick counts five silver back into your palm without a word. *(Out of game: your purse holds only gold, so she changed a piece for you.)* Then she reaches back into the common room, pulls a heel of bread off the end of a loaf on the counter and hands it to you. It's still warm. "Bread's with the room."

You tell her about the lad, quietly. She doesn't fold her arms this time. She looks past you at the gate and the ruts in the straw, and her mouth goes thin.

"Brown hair? Young?" She doesn't wait for you to answer. "Taerom's got two lads. Dunn's the elder, and nobody's seen him since the last load went out. Kell's the young one, and he's sixteen." She lets out a breath through her nose. "That'll be Kell. Daft, stubborn little…" She leaves it there.

She points out through the gate, to the right. "Thunderhammer Smithy. South along the street, the far side, past the cooper's. It's the big yard with the iron hammer hung over the gate, and you'll hear it before you see it. Taerom's the one with the beard and the temper." She looks you over again, boots to cloak, and this time she takes a little longer about it. "You tell him. He'll take it better from the man who saw it than from me." Then she goes back inside. The yard door stays open behind her.

The cat stops licking its paw.

*The wagon is slow,* it says. *I can still smell the horses on the street.*

+5 sps (Change from the gold piece for tonight's room (5 sp))
Journal: “The man under the iron wagon” updated

turns.message:
*Stay with me. We’ll find them together if it comes to that.*

I head straight to Thunderhammer Smithy at a brisk pace and ask for Taerom.

“James Worgen. I’ve just seen a brown-haired lad in a leather apron strapped beneath an iron wagon leaving the Anvil and Ember, heading north. He’s alive, and he put himself there deliberately. Mistress Hartwick thinks it’s Kell.” I pause. “She said you’re already missing an apprentice.”
turns.reply:
*Stay with me. We'll find them together if it comes to that.*

The cat doesn't answer. It falls in at your heel, tail up, and keeps pace through the straw and out of the gate.

Beregost's main street is busy now. Carts are coming in from the farms, an apprentice is sweeping cinders off a doorstep, and every forge you pass breathes heat at you. You go south past the cooper's, where a man is hammering hoops onto a barrel, and the next sound is heavier than all the rest. It's slow, even blows, a big hammer on a big anvil. Over a wide gateway hangs an iron hammer as long as a man's arm, black with age and swinging a little on its chain.

The Thunderhammer's yard is full of finished work: wagon tyres, plough-shares, a rack of hinges. Under the open shed a man is working at the anvil alone. He's barrel-chested, with a beard gone grey at the corners of his mouth and forearms scarred white from old burns. There's a second anvil beside him with a hammer laid across it, and nobody at it.

He doesn't look up until you say his name. Then he finishes the blow, lays the bar back in the coals and turns round.

You tell him. He listens with the hammer still in his fist. When you say *strapped beneath*, his jaw sets. When you say *north*, he shuts his eyes for a moment.

"Kell." It's barely a word. He puts the hammer down on the anvil very carefully, the way a man does when he wants to throw it. "That's Kell. Little fool. He said he would and I told him I'd tan him if he tried."

He wipes his hands on his apron. They aren't dirty.

"Dunn's his brother. My sister's boys. I've had them since they were this high." He holds a hand flat at his belt. "Those buyers came through three tendays back with the second load and said they wanted a hand at their works. Somebody who knew iron. A silver a day, paid ahead. Dunn's twenty and he's been wanting out from under me for a year, so he went. Said he'd be back in a tenday." Taerom looks at the empty anvil. "He wasn't."

"Grey-coat came back for this load last night. I asked him. He said Dunn's well, he's signed on for the season, and he gave me Dunn's wages to hold." His voice goes flat. "I took the money and I sold him the iron. Kell heard all of it." He lets out a breath. "Coast road. That's all Dunn ever got out of them. A work site on the coast road. They'll leave the Way north of town and turn west, toward the Cloakwood."

He's already moving. He pulls the apron over his head, throws it over the anvil and takes a short-hafted maul down from the wall.

"I've a cob in the back that'll carry me. She's not quick, but neither's that wagon." Then he stops and looks at you properly for the first time: the crossbow, the cloak, the soldier's way you're standing. "I can't pay you what a sellsword gets. There's Dunn's wages, and what's in the box." His mouth twists. "You saw him. Will you come?"
changes: Journal: “The man under the iron wagon” updated

turns.message:
“Yes. Keep the wages for Dunn.”

I step aside so he can get to the cob. “But keep that maul low when we catch them. We know Kell’s there; we don’t yet know what’s happened to his brother. Let’s not give those buyers a reason to take it out on either lad.”

I follow him towards the stable. “Can you lend me a mount nearby, or shall I keep pace on foot?”
turns.reply:
Taerom stops halfway to the back of the yard. "Keep the wages for Dunn." He says it back to you as if he's testing whether it holds, then gives one short nod and keeps going. He doesn't thank you.

He hears you out about the maul with his back to you. He's dragging a saddle off a peg in the lean-to, and it's an old one, cracked at the cantle. Behind it stands a broad grey cob with feathered feet and a sleepy eye. She lets him throw the saddle on without moving.

"Low." He hauls the girth tight, and the cob grunts. "Aye. I'll not swing at anybody while Kell's under that wagon." He buckles the strap and stays bent over it a moment longer than he needs to. "If they've done something to Dunn, I'll make you no promises. You'd best know that now."

He straightens up and hangs the maul from the saddle by a loop of rope through the haft, close to hand. Then he looks at you, at your boots, and out at the street.

"There's only her. She'll carry me and nothing else, and she won't go faster than a good walk. That wagon won't either, the way it's loaded." He jerks his chin north. "Feldepost's hires out hacks, at the top of the street where the caravans make up. It's on our road anyway. Old Feldepost charges a gold a day and more if he sees you're in a hurry, so don't look like you are. Or you walk beside me. A man on his feet keeps up with her fine. I've done it a hundred times, leading her to market."

He takes the cob's bridle and leads her out from under the lean-to. Her hooves are loud on the cinders.

The cat has gone ahead of you both. It sits on the gatepost under the old black hammer and looks north up the street.

*Horses, iron, the boy's smoke. Going away north,* it says. *Still on the big road.*

Taerom stops at the gate and waits for you.

 *(Out of game: that question needed no roll and it got its answer. Taerom has only the cob to lend, so the choice is yours: hire a hack at Feldepost's for about 1 gp, or walk beside him on foot. The turn stopped there so you could decide.)*
changes: Taerom Fuiruim takes off: Short-hafted maul
Changed: Short-hafted maul (Taerom hung it from the cob's saddle for the ride north.)
Promise: Ride with Taerom after the iron wagon
Journal: “The man under the iron wagon” updated

turns.message:
“I’ll walk. We’ve given them enough of a head start.”

I set off north beside Taerom, following the wagon’s route. *Keep a little ahead,* I ask the cat, *but stay within speaking distance. Let me know when you spot them.*

“Grey-coat have a name?” I ask Taerom as we go.
turns.reply:
The street is busier now. Taerom leads the cob at a steady walk, and the townsfolk step out of her way without being asked. The cat runs on ahead. It keeps to the edge of the street, past gutters and doorsteps, and stops now and then to wait until you're close enough again.

"Grey-coat have a name?"

Taerom doesn't answer right away. He walks on a few steps with the bridle in his fist.

"Sele. Master Sele." He says it like a word that tastes bad. "No first name. He chalked it on my tally board the first time, under the weight. Neat hand, like a clerk's." He glances at you. "Says he buys for a company. I asked him which one, the second time. He just smiled and paid."

The cob blows through her nose. Taerom goes on, quieter now.

"Twelve danters, he gave me for Dunn. For a season." His jaw works. "A silver a day doesn't come to twelve gold. Not in one season. I took it anyway."

The north end of the street opens up around Feldepost's, a long, low inn with a big yard. A Gate caravan is making up there: six wagons, oxen, a caravan master shouting over the noise. Nobody looks at two men on foot and a slow grey cob. Past the last smithy the houses thin out into hedged fields, and then the Trade Way runs on north across open country. It's packed earth with deep ruts, a low line of hills to the left, and the sun climbing.

You walk. The cat moves along the verge ahead of you, a dark spot in the long grass, sometimes on the road and sometimes off it. Taerom doesn't talk. Once he loosens the rope loop on the maul, then ties it back tight again.

It's past nine when the cat stops on the crest of a low rise, a couple of hundred feet ahead. It doesn't sit down.

*The wagon,* it says. *On the road, down the far side and out across the flat. Slow. The man on the mare rides behind it.* Its tail twitches. *The boy's smoke is still under it. He hasn't let go.*

A pause.

*The man on the mare looks back. Not often. He has done it twice.*

From where you are on the slope you can't see over the crest yet. Taerom has heard nothing, but he's watching your face, and he has stopped the cob.
changes: Changed: Dunn's wages (Taerom named the sum: twelve danters for a season.)
New place: The Trade Way north of Beregost

turns.message:
“They’re just over the rise. Kell’s still underneath.” I keep my voice low. “Let me do the talking. We’ll ask after Dunn first.”

*Come back to me,* I tell the cat.

I walk openly over the crest beside Taerom, hands clear of my weapons. Once we’re within easy calling distance, I hail the rider.

“Master Sele! A moment, please. Master Fuiruim and I would like a word about his nephew.”
turns.reply:
"Talk, then," Taerom says, just as low. He moves his hand off the saddle, well away from the maul, and grips the cob's bridle instead.

The cat leaves the crest and comes back down through the long grass. It falls in at your heel without a word.

You go over the rise together, in plain sight. The flat below is open country with hedgeless pasture on both sides and the Way running straight through it, rutted and pale in the sun. The wagon is a few hundred feet ahead, creeping along with the canvas swaying. The bearded driver is on the box and the other man walks at the lead horse's head. Sele rides behind on the dun mare.

He sees you before you've gone a dozen paces down the slope. He doesn't stop. He looks back once, a long, level look, then faces forward again and rides on at the wagon's pace. It takes most of a quarter of an hour on foot to close the gap. The cob plods along without hurrying. By the time you're near enough to call without shouting, you can hear the springs groaning under the iron.

"Master Sele! A moment, please. Master Fuiruim and I would like a word about his nephew."

Sele raises a gloved hand without turning, and the walking driver looks back. "Keep her moving, Orrin. I'll catch you up." The wagon rolls on. Sele turns the mare in the road and comes back towards you at a walk. He stops a little more than a spear's length off and stays in the saddle. His coat has fallen open on the right side, and his right hand rests on his thigh, close to it.

"Master Fuiruim." He nods to the smith, then looks at you. "And the gentleman from the window. I see Feldepost's had nothing going north." He doesn't smile, but he isn't unfriendly. "Dunn is well. He's at the works. He signed on for the season and put his mark to it, as I told Master Fuiruim last night, and I left his wages in good coin." He glances at Taerom. "I understand the young man's family would rather have him home. He's twenty, though, and the choice was his."

Taerom says nothing. A muscle moves in his jaw, and he keeps his eyes on the wagon getting smaller up the road.

Sele's eyes follow his, just for a moment, then come back to you.

"Was there something more? I'd rather not let the iron get too far ahead of me on an open road."

record.opening: Grey morning light slips through the shutter slats and falls across the plank floor. Somewhere down the street a smith's hammer has already started, steady as a heartbeat, and the smell of woodsmoke and frying bacon drifts up the stairs. The cat sits on the windowsill, tail curled around its paws, watching the door. Your purse sits heavy on the chair where you left it, about three hundred and fifty gold from the last hand you will ever play. Your gear is where you dropped it: crossbow, rod, the soldier's cloak over the bedpost. Your deck is still tied up in your pack. From the common room below comes laughter, the scrape of a bench, and the soft riffle of cards being shuffled, again and again. Then you notice it. Just inside the door, on the bare boards, lies a single playing card, face down. You don't remember it being there last night. The cat has not taken its eyes off it. Today, nobody is waiting on you. What do you do?

turns.message:
“Not playing,” I tell the cat. “Tidying.”

I crouch beside the card and turn it over by one corner, looking for any writing on it.
turns.reply:
James crouches, pinches one corner of the card between finger and thumb, and flips it over.

It's the Knave of Swords from a cheap tavern deck. The ink is worn grey along the edges where a lot of thumbs have held it. There's no writing on the face. Then he sees the top right corner: someone has pressed a fingernail into it and left a tiny crescent dent. You only feel it if you know to look. James knows. On the southern coast that nick told a dealer which cards were the high ones without him having to look. It's an old cheat's mark, and not a subtle one.

He turns it again. On the back, across the faded print, someone has written in soft charcoal, smudged where the card was slid under the door:

*Seat's warm. Bring the purse.*

There's no name and no signature.

The gap under the door is easily wide enough for a card to slide through. Downstairs the shuffling goes on, the same quick riffle and bridge over and over, like a man warming up his hands. Someone laughs. Orla's voice cuts through it, telling somebody to move his elbows off her clean table.

The cat drops off the windowsill without a sound, walks over and sniffs the card in James's fingers. Its whiskers go flat. It looks up at him, then sits down squarely in front of the door with its back to him.
changes: New place: Common room of the Lantern and Anvil

turns.message:
“Breakfast first. Bad decisions after.”

I dress and gather my gear, tucking the marked card away separately from my deck. Then I head downstairs with the cat, looking for Orla rather than the gaming table.

“Morning. Bacon and bread, please. Who’s been inviting himself to my purse?”
turns.reply:
James dresses without hurrying. Boots, the studded leather, the old Tethyrian cloak over his shoulders, the rod and the Lady's coin where his hand can find them. He slides the Knave into an inside pocket on its own, away from the tied-up deck in his pack. The cat waits by the door until he opens it, then goes down the stairs ahead of him with its tail up.

The common room smells of bacon fat and hot bread. A dozen people are in at this hour: carters eating fast, two smiths' apprentices with soot already in the creases of their knuckles, and an old man asleep over his porridge. The game is at the table nearest the hearth. There are four players. A lean man in his forties sits with his back to the wall, his hands moving through the deck in the same riffle and bridge James heard through the floor. Beside him a round-faced woman in a traveller's green coat laughs at something no one else found funny. Two locals make up the table, a wheelwright by the look of his forearms and a younger man who keeps checking his coins.

The lean man looks up as James reaches the bottom step. He smiles and lifts two fingers off the deck in a small wave, and his hands never stop. Then he goes back to dealing.

The cat jumps onto a stool at the end of the counter and sits there facing the hearth.

Orla Vance is behind the counter, carving a slab of bread with a knife half the length of her arm. She takes in James, the cat and the cat's stool in one look.

"Bacon and bread. Three silver, goes on your room." She slaps two rashers onto a plate from the pan behind her and saws off a thick end of the loaf. Then she leans in, and her voice drops for the first time all morning. "Inviting himself to your purse. Well, I didn't see anyone go up your stair, if that's what you're asking. I was in the kitchen since before light."

She pushes the plate across and tips her head a fraction toward the hearth table.

"That one with the cards came in three days back, off the south road. Plays every morning, pays for his ale, never makes trouble, so I don't ask. The laughing one in the green coat came in the same day, from the north, she says. Hessa. Separate rooms, and the two of them act like strangers." Orla wipes the knife on her apron. "Strangers who never once sit apart at that table. Funny, that."

Someone at the far end calls for more ale, and she straightens up.

"I've got a full room and one pair of hands. Eat your breakfast."

turns.message: I settle at the counter with my breakfast, angled so I can watch the game without approaching it. I’m looking for the dealer feeling marked corners, signals between him and Hessa, and whether they’re steering the losses toward the two locals.
turns.reply:
James takes his plate to the end of the counter by the cat's stool and sits half-turned, one elbow on the wood, the bread in his hand. From here the hearth table sits at the edge of his eye. It's the old way of watching a game you aren't in: you look at the fire, the door, the cat, and let the cards come to you.

The lean man deals. The young local picks his cards up too fast and holds them too close. The wheelwright sorts his slowly with one thick thumb. Hessa laughs at something before anyone has said anything.

He watches for four hands, maybe a quarter of an hour, and the dealer's hands beat him.

They're good hands, better than a tavern table deserves. The man deals low and close to his chest, the deck tipped toward himself, and from twelve feet away and side-on, James can't once catch a thumb going to a corner. Maybe it does and the angle hides it. Maybe it doesn't happen while somebody at the counter is paying attention. If he's passing anything to Hessa, James can't read it either. She touches her coat collar, tears her bread into pieces, laughs, leans on the wheelwright's shoulder. Any of that could be a signal or none of it. He can't tell from here.

The coins are easier to follow, and James can count them.

The young local is losing. It isn't much at a time, a few silver a hand, but his pile only shrinks. Every time he looks at it he does a small sum with his lips. The wheelwright is breaking about even and seems happy with that. Hessa takes one fat pot in the second hand with a shriek that turns heads at the carters' table, then loses most of it to the dealer two hands later. She shrugs it off cheerfully and ends up roughly where she started. The dealer wins steadily and modestly, never the biggest pot, never a hand that makes anyone stare.

James has played at tables like this, and he's run a few. The pattern fits a con. It also fits a run of bad luck for one young man. Nothing he's seen so far is anything he could swear to.

The cat isn't watching the cards. It's watching the young man's hands, the way it watches a mouse that hasn't realised it's being watched yet.

At the end of the fourth hand the dealer gathers the cards. Riffle, bridge. He doesn't look up, but his voice carries easily over the room.

"Room for a fifth, friend. Watching's free, but it's cold over there by the door."

Hessa laughs as if he's said something very funny, and pats the empty stool beside her.

 James lets the invitation hang and stays at the counter a moment longer. His read of the table has failed. Fifteen minutes of watching from the counter have given him nothing he could put a finger on. He hasn't seen a corner touched or caught one signal between the dealer and Hessa, and he still can't say whether anyone is steering the losses. He had the man's hands in plain view the whole time, and they gave him nothing.
changes: Playing cards (Wisdom +1, proficiency +3): reading the dealer's hands and the table from the counter: 13 vs 15 — failure

turns.message:
“No cards for me. I've discovered I like keeping my breakfast down.”

I take the marked Knave from my pocket and hold it up, charcoal message facing the dealer.

“But someone left this under my door. Was that you?”
turns.reply:
James lifts the Knave between two fingers and turns the charcoal toward the hearth table. Across the room, the dealer's hands go still on the deck for half a heartbeat, the first time they've stopped all morning.

Then the riffle picks up again, easy as before.

The man squints at the card like it's something curious a dog has dragged in. "Me? No, friend." He sounds sorry about it. "I don't need to slide notes under doors. I ask out loud, you heard me." He nods at the charcoal. "That's a better hand than mine, though. Somebody's been saving their pennies for lessons."

His face stays open and a little amused, and James can't find a crack in it. The man says it the way he'd say it was raining, and nothing in the denial snags.

Something else does, and it's on the table, not in his face. Four discarded cards lie face down by the wheelwright's elbow. Their backs are the same cheap tavern print as the Knave in James's hand: a faded grey lattice with a blot of a sun in the middle, worn pale at the edges. It's a common enough pattern. Orla probably sells decks like it over the counter for a few coppers, and half the inns on the Trade Way stock the same thing.

Hessa gets in before anyone else does. She throws her head back and laughs, loud enough that one of the carters turns round on his bench.

"Oh, *listen* to him! Somebody's sweet on you, love, that's all that is. I had a boy in Daggerford leave me a turnip on my windowsill every morning for a tenday." She pats the stool beside her again. "A card's a sight better than a turnip."

The wheelwright snorts into his ale. He couldn't care less.

The young man is a different matter. He's stopped doing sums with his lips. He's looking at the card in James's hand, and then, slowly, at the dealer's deck, then down at his own small pile of silver. He doesn't say anything. His ears have gone red.

On her stool by the counter, the cat yawns, showing every tooth.

The dealer squares the deck with a tap and starts the next deal. The cards go out low and quick: wheelwright, Hessa, the young man, himself. He leaves a gap where a fifth seat would be.

"Offer stands, friend," he says, not looking up. "Notes or no notes."

turns.message:
“Offer declined.”

I turn the Knave face out and run my thumbnail over its dented corner.

“This one’s marked. Old trick—lets a dealer feel a high card without seeing its face. Whoever sent the invitation has a peculiar sense of hospitality.”

I look toward the young man. “Might be worth checking the deck before you stake any more silver.”
turns.reply:
James turns the Knave so the room can see its face and draws his thumbnail slowly across the top right corner. In the quiet that follows, the little dent catches the firelight.

His voice carries well enough. At the carters' table, two men stop chewing.

The young man stares at the card and then at the deck squared under the dealer's palm. He has the look of someone adding up every hand he's lost this morning and not liking the total. He reaches across the table.

"Let's see 'em, then."

The dealer doesn't snatch the deck back. He lifts his hand off it slowly, all good humour, as if he'd been about to suggest the same thing. "Help yourself, friend. Every card in Orla's box has been bent by half of Beregost, mind."

The young man fans the cards out on the table and goes through them one at a time, pressing his thumb into each top right corner the way James did. He frowns. He goes back and does a few again.

He can't make it come out. The corners are soft and dog-eared, some bent, some creased, a couple torn right through. They're cheap cards that have been handled to death, and under his thumb a fingernail nick feels the same as ordinary wear. He holds two up to the window light and squints at them, then sets them down. His ears go redder still, and this time it looks more like embarrassment than anger.

"They're all dented," he mutters. "Every one."

"Told you, friend." The dealer spreads his hands. He isn't smiling now, and he's careful about that. He looks like a patient man who has just been called a cheat in front of a room and is choosing not to take offence. "No harm. Man gets a funny note under his door, he's going to see shadows."

Hessa laughs, a beat too loud, and starts gathering up her coins. "Well, that's put a chill on the morning, hasn't it! I ought to be off anyway, I've a cart to catch north before the road gets busy." She sweeps her silver into a purse and doesn't look at the dealer.

The wheelwright looks around, works out that the game is over, shrugs, and gets up to find more ale.

The dealer collects the scattered cards one-handed and squares them. His other hand is already scooping his winnings into a leather pouch, quick and neat. It's his first hurried movement all morning.

The young man doesn't look at either of them. He's turned on his stool toward the counter, toward James. He holds up one card from the spread, the Queen of Cups, by its corner. His voice drops so the whole room won't hear.

"Which ones, then? You said high cards. Show me what I'm feeling for."

On her stool, the cat has sat up straight and is watching the dealer's pouch.

turns.message:
I step over to the young man and set the Knave beside his Queen.

“A small crescent pressed into the corner, rather than a fold or a frayed edge. Here—feel this one. But a marked card under my door doesn't prove their deck is marked. I haven't caught anyone cheating.”

I keep my hands clear of his coins. “May I look at your Queen?”
turns.reply:
James crosses the few steps to the hearth table and sets the Knave face up on the boards beside the young man's Queen. Up close the table smells of spilled ale and woodsmoke. Dalmer is two feet away, tying off his pouch, and doesn't look over.

The young man takes the Knave in his hand and runs his thumb across the top right corner the way James showed him, slowly, then a second time. His mouth sets.

"That's not wear." He says it quietly, almost to himself. "That's a nail."

He looks at the Queen in his other hand for a moment, then holds it out to James by the edges, as if it might bite.

"Go on. Look."

James takes it to the window light and holds the two cards side by side. He tilts them so the light slides across their faces and feels each corner in turn with the pad of his thumb.

It's there.

The Queen's top right corner is as soft and grubby as every other card's in Orla's box, and under the thumb it feels like nothing. Tipped against the light, though, the crescent shows: a small curve pressed in from the face side, no wider than a fingernail. It sits in the same corner as the Knave's, at the same slant and about the same depth. They look like they were made by the same nail.

One more detail catches James's eye. The grime along the Queen's edges has gone grey and greasy from years of thumbs. Inside the little curve, the card is paler and cleaner, so whatever pressed it there did it recently, not years ago.

A low card would settle it. James doesn't have one in his hand, though. The rest of the deck is squared under Dalmer's palm, and Dalmer has just stood up.

He does it without hurrying. The pouch goes onto his belt and the deck goes into his coat, and he steps out from behind the table toward the stair, nodding pleasantly at the room. Near the door Hessa is buttoning her green coat with her back to all of them. She's taking her time over the buttons.

The young man hasn't looked away from James's face the whole time. Whatever he sees there, he doesn't wait for it to be said.

"It's on mine too," he says, low. "Isn't it."
changes: Playing cards: find the nail mark on the Queen of Cups, with the Knave beside it for comparison: 22 vs 10 — success
The nervous young man at the card table now has: Queen of Cups (marked card)
Lent: Queen of Cups (marked card) → James Worgen — The young local handed it over so James could look at it. Give it back to him. It comes from Dalmer's deck.
The card-player downstairs now has: Pouch of winnings

turns.message:
“Yes. Same crescent, freshly pressed.” I hand him back his Queen.

“Dalmer,” I call, plainly enough for Orla to hear. “This Queen has the same fresh mark as the Knave. Leave the deck on the table so we can compare the low cards. If it’s ordinary wear, that should clear things up.”

I stay beside the table, hands empty.
turns.reply:
A quick correction before the scene: in my last narration I called the card-player "Dalmer," but nobody at the table had said his name aloud. That was my mistake. We'll say James heard the wheelwright call him by it over the cards. It counts as known from here on.

---

James hands the Queen back. The young man takes it by the edges and holds it a moment, looking down at the corner.

"Dalmer." James doesn't raise his voice much, but in a room this quiet it doesn't need raising. "This Queen has the same fresh mark as the Knave. Leave the deck on the table so we can compare the low cards. If it's ordinary wear, that should clear things up."

Dalmer is on the second stair. He stops there with one hand on the rail and turns around slowly, a man who's been called back for something he forgot.

Before he gets a word out, the street door bangs. A breath of cold air comes in with the ring of the forges. Hessa's stool by the door is empty, and through the front window the green coat is already past the horse trough, walking north.

Nobody in the room watches her go except James and the cat.

Orla comes out of the kitchen doorway, drying her hands on her apron. She has heard every word.

"Compare what with what?"

"His deck," the young man says. His voice has stopped shaking. "He said it was yours. Said half of Beregost bent it."

Orla looks at Dalmer, then reaches under the counter without hurrying and pulls out a shallow drawer. Two decks sit in it, each tied with a bit of string, with the same grey lattice and blot of a sun on the backs. She sets them on the counter side by side.

"I keep two. They're both here." She closes the drawer. "Whatever he's got in his coat, he didn't get it from me."

That changes the room. At the carters' table a big man in a leather apron puts down his spoon and stands up. He doesn't come any closer. He just stands there. The wheelwright stays by the ale barrel, but he's turned to watch.

Dalmer takes all of it in: the drawer, the carter, the empty stool by the door. James can see him decide. His hand doesn't go to the dagger at his belt. It goes to the pouch.

"Well." He comes down one stair, not both, and unties the pouch in his palm. "Bought it off a pedlar, as it happens, and I'll grant you he may have been a sharper man than me. I won't have it said I took a Beregost lad's silver in a bad deck." He looks at the young man. "What was it, friend? Fourteen? Fifteen?"

"Sixteen," the young man says.

Dalmer counts sixteen silver pieces onto the newel post one at a time, and every one clicks on the wood. Then he ties the pouch off again, with the rest of the morning's winnings still in it, and the deck stays inside his coat.

"For the peace of the house." He looks past the young man, over Orla's counter, and settles on James. He's still pleasant, but there's nothing easy in it now. "The lad's whole again, and I'm out of your inn inside the hour. That's fair, isn't it?"

The young man doesn't move toward the silver. He's looking at James.

On her stool, the cat has turned around to face the stair.
changes: Returned: Queen of Cups (marked card) → The nervous young man at the card table

Lies here: Common room of the Lantern and Anvil receives 16 sps (Dalmer counted the young local's 16 silver onto the newel post at the foot of the stair, «for the peace of the house». Nobody has taken it yet.)
Orla Vance now has: Lattice-and-sun tavern deck ×2
New person: The carter in the leather apron

turns.message:
“The lad can speak for his silver, and Orla for her house. But that deck shouldn't find another table.”

I nod toward his coat. “Leave it with Orla, return anything else you won this morning, and I'll have no further quarrel with you.”
